This metaphor comes from Harvard scholar Sunstein's "Information Utopia" in 2006; it is also similar to the "Filter Bubble" (emphasis on the filtering effect of the algorithm) and the "Echo Chamber" (Echo Chamber, emphasizing the reinforcement of opinions within the group) proposed by Pariser in 2011. The three have different sources and have different emphases, and are often used interchangeably on a daily basis.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "what is recommended to me is the most important"; or completely denying the recommendation algorithm and ignoring its efficiency value.
fields.典型案例: Compare the differences in recommendation results for the same topic under different accounts and discuss why you see different results.
fields.反例: Think of "the most popular ones" as "the true thoughts of the majority of people."
fields.深度上限: Only the intuition of causes and self-examination methods will be discussed, and the specific model mechanism of the recommendation algorithm will not be discussed.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Not scapegoating algorithms, nor denying personal responsibility in information selection.
fields.教学类比: Like "you only eat what you like, and you end up with nutritional imbalances", but the canteen menu is created by an algorithm.
fields.来源依据: Sunstein "Information Utopia" (2006); Pariser "Filter Bubble" (2011); Tencent Research Institute "Algorithm Breaking the Cocoon" (2025); Master §3.1 K6 "Public Impact"
fields.通俗解释:
The platform keeps an eye on your clicks and stays, constantly pushing similar content. The more you watch, the more similar the content will be. In the end, the information you are exposed to becomes narrower and narrower. This is an "information cocoon". It's like choosing only what you like to eat, and ending up with nutritional imbalances, but this menu is created by an algorithm. Similar terms include "filter bubbles" and "echo chambers". One emphasizes algorithmic filtering, and the other emphasizes mutual reinforcement in a circle. They are often used interchangeably.
Both biases must be guarded against. First, don’t think that “what’s recommended to me is the most important.” Recommendations only mean that you like to watch them; secondly, don’t completely deny the recommendation algorithm. Its efficiency is real, and the problem is that it only feeds you what you like to eat.
There is a stupid way to self-examine: search the same topic on another account, compare the difference between the two recommendation results, and think about why you see different results. Don’t take the popular ones you see as the true thoughts of the majority of people. The menu is created by an algorithm, but you still use the chopsticks.

fields.精确定义: A database dedicated to storing and retrieving vector representations, using similarity (rather than exact match) to find semantically similar content.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
Most people have heard of databases, but they may not be familiar with databases that specifically store vectors. It stores a vector representation, that is, a string of values ​​into which the content is converted; when searching, it is not an exact match, but similarity is calculated to find content with similar semantics.
Ordinary databases are like roll call by name. Only when the correct name is called will someone answer the call. If there is even one word difference, the result may be checked. The vector database takes a different approach, like finding a person by appearance: the query also becomes a vector, and the distance between the two sides is compared, and the one closest to you comes out first. Even if the original words do not overlap even one word, and the meaning is similar, it still hits the target.
Its use lies in "finding meaning": the content is first converted into a vector and stored, and when the need arises, you can browse it according to the similarity, and you can quickly get the ones with similar semantics.

fields.精确定义: Force the model to be output according to the specified structure (such as JSON Schema), which facilitates stable parsing and downstream use of the program.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
The model usually speaks freely, and the program becomes a headache to read. Structured output solves this trouble: define a format in advance, such as JSON Schema, and force the model to answer according to this structure. There are rules for what fields should be put.
Once the structure is fixed, the downstream will have less worries. The program directly parses the output after receiving it, and takes values ​​from field to field. There is no need to worry about the model saying one more sentence this time and one less answer next time. The data will be transmitted back, entered into the system, and fed to the next link.
Free answers are like a handwritten note, no matter how good the handwriting is, it still needs someone to read it; structured output is like a form filled in according to the form, the grid is locked, and the machine can be used as soon as it is brought.

fields.精确定义: A question and answer system built based on internal enterprise documents usually consists of RAG plus permission management and evaluation.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
There are piles of documents in the company: systems, manuals, and process descriptions, and employees often spend a long time looking through them to find answers. Enterprise knowledge Q&A is a Q&A system based on internal documents. When employees ask a question, it finds evidence from the documents and gives an answer.
Such a set is usually a combination of three things: Retrieval Enhanced Generation (RAG) is responsible for finding information and organizing answers; authority management is responsible for checking who can check which documents are not messy; evaluation is responsible for acceptance, and someone is watching whether the answers are accurate and stable.
It is like setting up a consultation desk in the company to answer all questions. The "consultant" behind the desk only reads the company's own documents. The source of the answers can be checked, and there is no need to figure it out on your own.

fields.精确定义: Measure the extent to which model outputs appear reasonable but are actually incorrect, and establish verification mechanisms.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
AI sometimes says the wrong things seriously: it sounds smooth and reasonable, but it is actually made up. This content that seems reasonable but is actually wrong is called an illusion. The difficulty in preventing it is that it "looks right". If you don't check it, it is easy to be passed over. Like a coherent wrong answer on a test paper, the smoother it is, the more likely it is to deceive the examiner.
There must be a way to measure how many hallucinations there are and how wrong they are. This is factual evaluation: to measure the extent of such erroneous content in the model output, and then build a verification mechanism so that errors can be discovered and stopped.
Use the materials provided by AI, don’t assume they are correct by default. A smooth answer does not mean a true answer. Important content must still be checked from the source. Assessment and verification are not decorations, they are necessary actions that are used every day.

2-22.name: Watermarking and Content Provenance — C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity)

fields.精确定义: Embed invisible watermarks or encrypted signature metadata in AI-generated content, and record the source and modification history for verification.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
Is a video or article made by a human or generated by AI? It becomes increasingly difficult to tell with the naked eye. The method is to put marks into the content: embed invisible watermarks in AI-generated content, or add encrypted signature metadata, record the source and modification history on the content itself, and use it for verification when necessary.
The division of labor between the two methods is different. The watermark is hidden inside the content, invisible to the naked eye, but can still be recognized; the signature metadata is like an accompanying factory receipt, recording where it comes from and what has been changed in the process.
With these records, the origin of the content can be traced and its authenticity can be verified. Determining whether a piece of material was generated by AI and who has modified it depends on checking records, not guessing.

fields.精确定义: A set of clear, limited, actionable steps to solve a type of problem.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "algorithms must be implemented by computers" (algorithms are method descriptions and can exist without computers).
fields.典型案例: Fixed steps for organizing school bags; express sorting rules.
fields.反例: Think of "empirical randomization" as an algorithm.
fields.深度上限: Only the identification of "clear, limited, and repeatable steps" is done, without complexity analysis.
fields.通俗解释:
An algorithm is not something profound, it is just a set of steps to solve a certain type of problem: clearly written, with a limited number of steps, and each step can be followed. There is a set of fixed steps for sorting school bags, and there is a set of sorting rules for sorting packages at express delivery stations. These are all algorithms, and you don’t need to touch a computer from beginning to end.
Seize three conditions: the steps are clearly written and you will not get stuck if you follow them; there are a number of steps and you will not never finish them; each step can be actually executed without ambiguity. Only when these three conditions are met can it be considered an algorithm. If you handle it casually based on experience, if the steps are unclear, it doesn't count.
A common misunderstanding is this: thinking that algorithms must rely on computers to be established. In fact, it is the method itself. The recipe-like step description is the algorithm, and the computer is just a tool to execute it.

fields.精确定义: A basis for judgment or operation in the form of "if...then..." clearly set by a person.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "AI relies entirely on human-written rules" (in machine learning, rules are obtained from data statistics rather than all manually written).
fields.典型案例: Automatic control rule "If the temperature is higher than 30°C, turn on the fan".
fields.反例: I thought spam filtering relied entirely on people writing keywords one by one.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "conditional judgments clearly written by people", not the rule engine.
fields.安全与伦理边界: People must be able to explain the basis for the rules and be responsible for the consequences of the rules.
fields.来源依据: Master §3.2 Depth Cap: “Fixed Rules or Algorithmic Steps” vs. “Models Form Patterns from Data”
fields.通俗解释:
"When the temperature is higher than 30°C, turn on the fan." The basis for this judgment is the rules: clearly written by people, what actions should be taken when encountering the situation, each one is clear. Its form is "if...then...", which people can understand and check.
Rules are not the same thing as "laws learned by machines themselves". Some people think that AI relies entirely on humans writing rules one by one, but that is not entirely true: in tasks such as spam filtering, many judgments are made by the system from a large number of examples, rather than manually written keywords one by one.
The rules are set by people, and the responsibility falls on them: you can tell why this rule is set, and you have to admit it if something goes wrong.

fields.精确定义: The process of systematically searching for a solution that satisfies the goal in the space of possible solutions, such as path search and game tree search.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "search means searching for information on the Internet" (in AI, it refers to the systematic search of the solution space).
fields.典型案例: Find the shortest path in a maze; a chess program lists moves.
fields.反例: Think of "just try a few times" as a system search.
fields.深度上限: It only provides an intuitive experience of “listing possible options and then filtering them”, without mentioning the name and complexity of the search algorithm.
fields.来源依据: General content for introduction to AI
fields.通俗解释:
The search mentioned here is not about searching for information online. Search in AI refers to systematically finding the solution that satisfies the goal among a large number of possible methods. If you want to find the shortest route through a maze, you will check each fork in the road one by one; if you want to decide which move to take in a chess program, you will list the possible moves and deduce them one by one.
The key lies in the word "system". Just trying a few times to try your luck is not a search; listing the possible options, then filtering them one by one according to the target, and filtering out the one that can be used is. Path search and move deduction in chess programs all follow this path.
When you hear "AI can search" in the future, first think about whether it is searching web pages or a bunch of possible solutions. These two searches are not the same thing.

fields.精确定义: Computational structures (mathematical functions with parameters) learned from data that map inputs to outputs.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "the model is the 'brain' or entity of AI" (the model is a collection of parameters and operational structures, without subjective experience).
fields.典型案例: A computational structure that maps pictures into "cat/dog" judgments.
fields.反例: Talk about the model as "it learned" and "it figured it out."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the "input→output calculation structure" and does not talk about the details of the network structure.
fields.安全与伦理边界: The model may have errors and the output needs to be verified.
fields.通俗解释:
The word model sounds mysterious, but it is actually a mathematical structure that can do calculations: learn it from the data and turn input into output. Give it a picture, and it will spit out a judgment of "cat" or "dog". The work done in the middle is calculated according to a set of functions with parameters.
Note that it is not a "brain". A model is a collection of parameters and operational structures. It has no subjective experience. Emotional statements such as "it learned" and "it figured it out" are not appropriate. It is just calculating.
It also makes errors, and the output must be checked before being used. It is much more reliable to think of it as a machine that "gives you what you input according to the formula" than as a "brain that thinks about things".

fields.精确定义: Attributes or quantities used to describe samples and calculated by the model, such as height, pixel value, and word frequency.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "features must be manually specified by humans" (in deep learning, features can be extracted by the model itself).
fields.典型案例: Two types of leaves are distinguished based on "length and width".
fields.反例: Use task-irrelevant attributes (such as numbers) as features.
fields.深度上限: We only talk about "which attributes are used to judge", not feature engineering.
fields.安全与伦理边界: If the characteristics contain personal information, you need to be careful and avoid using sensitive attributes to make judgments.
fields.通俗解释:
To judge something, you must look at several indicators. These attributes used to describe samples and be calculated by the model are called features: height is a feature, the pixel value in the picture is a feature, and the number of times a word appears in an article is also a feature. For example, to distinguish two types of leaves, it is enough to look at the length and width. These two numbers are the characteristics.
Not all attributes can be used as features. Things that have nothing to do with the task will not work: give students numbers. Numbers are not helpful in judging anything, and there is no point in using them as features.
Another point: Features do not necessarily have to be manually selected. In deep learning, the model can extract useful features from the original data. In addition, if the characteristics contain personal information, you must be cautious, and you cannot use sensitive attributes to judge people.

fields.精确定义: A general term for methods that allow computers to automatically discover patterns from data and make predictions or judgments about new data accordingly, rather than having humans write rules one by one.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is "machine learning = robot learning actions"; or "machine learning is all of AI" (ML is a large category of AI methods).
fields.典型案例: After seeing a large number of email examples, the system learns to determine which ones look like spam.
fields.反例: I thought that people wrote every rule into the system.
fields.深度上限: It only makes an intuitive comparison of "examples → find patterns → use new examples", and does not talk about algorithm names and mathematics.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Patterns learned from data will bring bias in the data into the results.
fields.教学类比: The teacher gives examples and allows students to summarize the rules themselves, instead of copying the rules to students; but the machine does not "understand" but only calculates.
fields.来源依据: Master §3.2 "Differences between Fixed Rules and Model Generation"
fields.通俗解释:
Machine learning is a large category of methods in AI. The approach is the opposite of writing a program: Instead of humans writing the rules one by one, the computer is given a bunch of data and allowed to find patterns on its own. The patterns it finds are then used to deal with new data. After seeing a large number of email examples, the system will be able to judge by itself which emails look like spam. No one has ever written a rule for it such as "when certain words appear, it is spam."
It's a bit like the teacher doesn't copy the rules to the students, but only gives a bunch of examples for students to summarize on their own. But there is one difference that must be remembered: the machine does not "understand", it does calculations.
Two misunderstandings are easily cleared: machine learning is not a robot learning to perform actions; it is not equal to all of AI, but is just a large category of AI methods. Also, patterns are learned from data, and deviations in the data will also be incorporated into the results.

fields.精确定义: Supervised learning uses labeled data to train the model so that it learns to predict labels from the input; unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data and allows the model to discover structures or groupings in the data on its own.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "supervised learning requires someone to keep an eye on it" ("supervision" refers to label information); "unsupervised learning means that no one is in charge and you can learn randomly."
fields.典型案例: Exercises with answers (supervised) and automatic grouping of similar students (unsupervised).
fields.反例: Talk about unlabeled data as having standard answers.
fields.深度上限: We only distinguish between "whether there is a ready answer" and not about the algorithm family.
fields.通俗解释:
There is only one difference between the two learning methods: whether there is a ready-made answer. Supervised learning uses labeled data, and each example is accompanied by a correct answer. The model learns "what kind of output should be given when seeing such input", like doing exercises with answers. Unsupervised learning does not have the answer in hand, only a pile of raw data, allowing it to find out the structure and grouping within it, like automatically grouping students with similar interests into a pile.
The word "supervision" is easy to misunderstand: it does not mean someone standing by and watching, it means that the data contains label information. Don't think that unsupervised means that no one is in charge and you learn randomly. It is still calculated according to a fixed method.
Remember this line: those with standard answers are called supervised learning, those without standard answers are called unsupervised learning, and other usages can easily confuse it.

fields.精确定义: Neural network is a computing model composed of multiple layers of simple computing units connected to each other. It learns mapping relationships from data by adjusting connection weights; deep learning is a method that uses multi-layer neural networks to extract features layer by layer from original data.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "neural networks imitate the real structure of the human brain and can think like a brain" (it is only a mathematical structure inspired by biological neurons); the misunderstanding is that "deep learning = understanding".
fields.典型案例: Most models that can recognize faces and generate images are based on neural networks.
fields.反例: Say "AI neurons think like humans."
fields.深度上限: Only establish the age-appropriate intuition of "forming patterns from examples" without talking about network layers, parameters and backpropagation.
fields.教学类比: The statement "like a brain" can only be used to explain the source of inspiration, and it must be pointed out that the operating mechanism is different from that of the human brain.
fields.通俗解释:
Neural network is a computing model: many simple computing units are connected layer by layer, and the corresponding relationship between input and output is learned from the data by adjusting the connection weights between the units. Deep learning uses a neural network with more layers to extract features layer by layer from the original data. Today's models that can recognize faces and generate images are mostly built on this structure.
With "nerve" in the name, it is easy to be led astray. It is only inspired by biological neurons, and its operating mechanism is completely different from that of the human brain. It cannot be said to "think like a brain." Saying "the neurons of AI are thinking" is similar to saying "the filament of a desk lamp is thinking". It sounds like it, but it's not.
The equation "deep learning equals understanding" is also not true: it extracts patterns formed from examples, which is still far from understanding.

fields.精确定义: Training is the process of using data to adjust model parameters so that the output gradually approaches the target result; inference is the process of using fixed parameters to calculate the output for new inputs after training is completed. How do you know where to adjust training? Compare the gap between the output and the target, and continuously fine-tune according to the gap - this is the basic principle of training (professionally called "loss function and gradient descent", this course will not expand on it).
fields.常见误解: Confusing "training" and "inference"; misunderstanding that the model is still learning during inference (inference does not update parameters).
fields.典型案例: "Practice questions in daily life" is like training, and "answer questions in exams" is like inference.
fields.反例: I think the AI gets smarter every time you ask a question.
fields.深度上限: Only two stages are distinguished, and the training cycle and optimization algorithm are not discussed.
fields.安全与伦理边界: The source of training data must be legal; the personal information entered by inference must be protected.
fields.通俗解释:
The life of a model is divided into two stages. The first stage is called training: feed it data, compare its output with the target, and fine-tune it back as much as it is different. Round by round, the parameters are slowly adjusted until the output is close to the target. The last stage is called inference: after training, the parameters are fixed and an output is calculated based on this set of set parameters when new input comes. Daily practice questions correspond to training, and examination questions correspond to inference.
Distinguishing these two paragraphs can solve a popular misunderstanding: it does not mean that every time you ask the AI ​​a question, it will become smarter. You ask it and the answer is based on inference, and none of the parameters are changed. The model becomes stronger through the training phase, not through chatting with users.
By the way, two things: the data used for training must come from legal sources; the personal information entered during inference should also be protected.

fields.精确定义: In the interaction with the environment, the agent tries different actions and adjusts its strategy according to the reward signal to maximize the long-term cumulative reward learning method.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "reinforcement learning means repeated practice and rote memorization" (the core is to adjust the strategy based on reward signals).
fields.典型案例: The training program plays mini-games, and if the score is high, the corresponding practices will be strengthened.
fields.反例: Think of "practice more times" as reinforcement learning.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "trial and error + reward adjustment" and does not talk about policy gradient and Q function.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Reward settings are determined by people, and bad behavior will be learned if improperly set.
fields.来源依据: General content of machine learning; RLHF is its large model application (see 4-05)
fields.通俗解释:
The method of reinforcement learning is trial and error: an agent tries different actions in the environment, and is rewarded if it does well, and is not given or punished if it does poorly. It adjusts its strategy step by step according to the reward signal, with the goal of earning the most long-term accumulated rewards. The mini-games played by the training program are typical examples: whichever set of practices has a high score will be strengthened.
It's not as simple as "practice a few more times." Mere repetition without reward signals to guide adjustments is not reinforcement learning. The core lies in "adjusting strategies according to rewards".
Another thing to remember: rewards are set by humans. If not set properly, the program may learn messy behavior. How the reward is given determines what it learns.

fields.精确定义: Classification is to divide the input into preset categories (such as determining whether an email is spam); clustering is to automatically group similar samples into a group without giving a category in advance.
fields.常见误解: Confusing "classification" and "clustering" (classification has default categories, clustering has no default categories).
fields.典型案例: Classify photos into "cats/dogs" (categorization); automatically group students according to their interests (clustering).
fields.反例: Treat the automatic grouping results as predetermined categories.
fields.深度上限: We only compare two types of tasks and do not talk about algorithm implementation.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Clustering results may form inappropriate divisions of the population and should be interpreted with caution.
fields.通俗解释:
These two names are like twins, the difference lies in whether the category has been determined in advance. Classification is to classify input into pre-set categories: to determine whether an email is spam, the categories have already been determined, and there are only two categories. Clustering works in reverse: no categories are given in advance, and the system automatically groups similar samples into a bunch. No one knows in advance what the clustering will look like.
Let's take a pair of examples for comparison: classifying photos into "cats" or "dogs" is classification; automatically grouping the whole class according to interests, and only telling them in advance that they will be divided according to similarity, and then dividing into several groups and what each group will be called. It is not known until after the classification is completed. This is clustering.
Treating the clustering results as predetermined categories is the most common confusion. Be careful when using clustering on people. Automatic grouping may result in improper division of certain groups of people. Be careful when interpreting the results.

fields.精确定义: A pattern is a regular structure that appears repeatedly in the data and can be identified or used for prediction; the presence of correlation in the data does not mean the existence of a causal relationship.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "finding patterns is equivalent to finding causal relationships."
fields.典型案例: Ice cream sales are rising at the same time as the number of drownings, and the real reason is that the weather is getting hotter.
fields.反例: Because "both change together" it is asserted that "A causes B".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "changing together ≠ cause and effect" and does not talk about statistical inference methods.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Using correlations to make decisions may harm certain groups of people, so caution is required.
fields.通俗解释:
Regular structures that appear repeatedly in data and can be identified or predicted are called patterns. But remember one thing: two things changing together does not mean who caused the other. Correlation does not equal causation.
Classic example: On days when ice cream sales increase, the number of drownings tends to increase. The two do change together, but no one is responsible for the other. The reason behind it is that the weather is getting hotter: when the weather is hot, more people eat ice cream and more people swim in the water.
AI is good at finding patterns in data, but most of what it finds are correlations. If we assert that "A causes B" because "the two change together" and then use it to make decisions, it may actually hurt some people. Changing together is just the starting point, not the conclusion.

fields.精确定义: Probability is a numerical measure of how likely an event is to occur, expressed as a value from 0 to 1. Uncertainty is a lack of certainty about an outcome; it can arise from noisy data or limitations in a model’s capabilities.
fields.常见误解: “A model’s probability estimate tells us how often it is actually correct.” It represents the model’s confidence based on its training, and that confidence may be poorly calibrated. Another misconception is that AI outputs are always certain.
fields.典型案例: A weather forecast reports a 60% chance of rain.
fields.反例: Assuming that an AI answer must be correct simply because it sounds confident.
fields.深度上限: Use comparisons, simple counting, and boundary cases, without introducing formal statistical formulas.
fields.安全与伦理边界: When outcomes are uncertain, people must remain responsible for important decisions.
fields.来源依据: Course master document, §3.4, shared boundaries, item 3.
fields.通俗解释:
Probability describes how likely something is to happen, using a number between 0 and 1. In the model being used, 0 means impossible and 1 means certain; values in between describe different degrees of likelihood. A forecast giving a 60% chance of rain is one everyday example. Uncertainty means we cannot be sure of an outcome. It can come from noise in the data or limitations in the model.
One distinction matters: a model’s estimated probability is not automatically its real-world accuracy. It reflects confidence based on training, and that confidence may not be well calibrated.
An AI can sound certain and still be wrong. Confident wording is not evidence that an answer is correct. When the outcome is uncertain and the decision matters, a person needs to make the final judgment.

fields.精确定义: The ability of a model to perform well on new data that it has not seen during training.
fields.常见误解: Misunderstood as "remembering the performance of training samples" (on the contrary, generalization emphasizes adaptation to new data).
fields.典型案例: After learning to recognize the common characteristics of "cats", you can recognize pictures of cats you have never seen before.
fields.反例: Treating success on memorized questions as proof of ability on new ones.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "is it okay to use a new example?" and does not talk about generalization theory.
fields.教学类比: A student who memorizes answers may struggle when the question changes—an analogy for overfitting. A student who understands the idea can apply it to new questions. Generalization is about this second ability.
fields.通俗解释:
Generalization refers to the ability of the model to still perform well on new data that it has never seen before: examples that have not been seen during training still perform well. This is called generalization. After learning to recognize the common characteristics of "cats", you can also recognize a picture of a cat you have never seen before, relying on it.
It's the opposite of "memorize training examples". For example, students who memorize by rote know all the questions they have passed and are dumbfounded when they change the question type. This is called overfitting; students who really understand can draw inferences about other cases. Generalization is about the latter ability.
So don’t praise a model by saying “it knows all the test questions”, as that doesn’t reflect its true level. It only counts if you try a new example and see if it works.

fields.精确定义: The process of measuring model performance using independent data and clear metrics. When evaluating, count "right things as wrong" and "wrong things as right" separately, and then look at the proportion of right and wrong - the costs of the two types of errors are often different, depending on which scenario you are more afraid of.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "just look at a few examples and it feels accurate" (it needs to be systematically evaluated using prescribed indicators and independent test sets).
fields.典型案例: Use a batch of pictures that did not participate in training to measure the recognition accuracy.
fields.反例: Just pick a few successful cases to prove "good results".
fields.深度上限: Comparison of results and simple counting are used, without formal statistical evaluation.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Do not use "pretty cases" as a substitute for system evaluation or exaggerate capabilities.
fields.来源依据: Master §3.2 Depth upper limit; §3.4 Unified boundary
fields.通俗解释:
To evaluate a model, you cannot rely on feeling. The formal approach is to take a batch of independent data that has not participated in training and measure it according to clear indicators. For example, if you use a batch of pictures that have not been trained to measure the recognition accuracy, the measured numbers will be convincing. If you take the test again with the questions you have already taken, no matter how high your score is, it will still be an illusion. Only by taking the questions you have never seen before can you see your true level.
There is a point when counting: count "right as wrong" and "wrong as right" separately. The costs of these two types of mistakes are often different. Which one is more important depends on the specific scenario.
On the other hand, just picking a few successful cases and saying "the effect is good" does not count as evaluation. Beautiful cases cannot replace system evaluation, and using them to exaggerate capabilities is a bad idea.

fields.精确定义: Boundary cases refer to input situations outside the normal range or extreme; reliability testing refers to using normal, boundary and abnormal inputs to test whether the system is stable and whether the results are trustworthy.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "if it works under normal circumstances, it is reliable"; "testing means just trying it casually".
fields.典型案例: Test whether the translation tool will crash when it encounters blank input, long input, or garbled characters.
fields.反例: Only test with the most standard examples.
fields.深度上限: It only designs and records three types of use cases: "normal/boundary/abnormal" and does not talk about stress testing projects.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Failure situations must be recorded and explained, and must not be wrapped in success stories.
fields.通俗解释:
Just because a system is easy to use, does not mean it is reliable. What the reliability test needs to do is to feed it three types of inputs to see the reaction: normal, borderline, and abnormal. Boundary cases are those inputs that are outside the normal range and are more extreme. When testing a translation tool, you have to try blank input, long text, and garbled characters to see if it crashes.
Just take the most standard example and test it once and declare "no problem", which is equivalent to not testing it. "If it works under normal circumstances, it means it is reliable" and "Testing means just trying it casually." These two sentences are both misunderstandings.
There is also a hard requirement: failure situations in the test must be recorded and explained clearly. Packing only success stories and hiding the appearance of overturning is worse than the failure itself.

fields.精确定义: The empirical rule that model performance can predictably improve as the amount of parameters, data, and calculations increases; in recent years, it has also been found that using calculations to "think more when answering difficult questions" can also improve performance. Chinese also translates "law of scale" and "law of scale", which refer to the same concept.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "as long as the model is bigger, it will be better" (data quality, task type and inference period calculation are equally important).
fields.典型案例: Models in the same series are usually larger and more powerful, but also cost more.
fields.反例: Think of "more parameters" as "must be more reliable".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the qualitative understanding of "the existence of laws of scale and effect" and does not talk about the power law formula.
fields.安全与伦理边界: The larger the scale, the higher the energy consumption, which needs to be weighed against the environmental costs.
fields.来源依据: Kaplan et al. "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (2020); Hoffmann et al. Chinchilla (2022)
fields.通俗解释:
The scaling law refers to an empirical rule: model performance will increase as the amount of parameters, data, and calculations increase, and the improvement will be predictable. It is also translated as "law of scale" and "law of scale" in Chinese, which refers to the same concept. For models in the same series, the larger the scale, the stronger the capabilities, but at the expense of higher costs.
In recent years, we have also discovered that spending calculations on "thinking more when answering difficult questions" can also improve performance without necessarily making the model itself larger.
Therefore, "As long as it is bigger, it will be better" cannot be established. Data quality, task type, and computing power usage during the inference period are all involved; conversely, "the more parameters, the more reliable it will be" is also taken for granted. There are also accounts to be calculated: the larger the scale, the higher the energy consumption, and there are environmental costs.

fields.精确定义: Determine whether a certain task is suitable for AI, which one to use, and which steps should not be left to AI, based on the task objectives, data conditions, risks, and human needs.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "AI should be used wherever it can be used"; or "AI cannot be used at all if it is not suitable".
fields.典型案例: Calculating weather and humidity: an ordinary calculator is sufficient and does not require AI; AI is helpful when writing the first draft of an event notice.
fields.反例: Using AI for the sake of using AI will make it slower and worse.
fields.深度上限: It only makes judgments about "should it be used and in which step", not system architecture selection.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Do not leave decisions involving high-risk judgments (health, legal, financial, personal safety) to AI.
fields.来源依据: Master Version §1.5 "No AI Control Inspection" + §5.1 Scene Adaptation
fields.通俗解释:
AI should not be used everywhere. Before you start, make a judgment call: Is this task suitable for AI? Which one is suitable? Which steps should not be left to it at all? The basis for judgment is mission objectives, data conditions, risk levels, and actual needs of people.
Let’s take a pair of comparative examples: to calculate the weather and humidity, an ordinary calculator is enough, but using AI is a complete detour; when writing a first draft of an event notice, AI can really help. Using AI for the sake of using AI ends up being slow and poor.
Two red lines are clearly drawn: first, don’t think that “it should be used wherever it can be used”; second, don’t beat it to death with a stick. Just because this scenario is inappropriate does not mean that AI cannot be used anywhere. Especially for high-risk matters, such as health, legal, financial, and personal safety, the decision-making power must be left in the hands of people.

fields.精确定义: The overall design method of "how information flows and how to calculate" within the model. Different architectures are suitable for different tasks, which is a common superordinate concept for the classification of various models such as large models and image models.
fields.常见误解: Confusing "architecture" with "model size" and "model capabilities".
fields.典型案例: Put Transformer, diffusion model, and MoE into the category of "architecture" and understand "different approaches to the same type of things."
fields.反例: Say "changed the architecture" as "changed the model file".
fields.深度上限: It only establishes the classification intuition that "architecture is a type of design method" and does not talk about specific structural details.
fields.教学类比: Just like the "house design" of a house: it can be lived in the same way, but the structure is different, and it is suitable for different people and uses.
fields.通俗解释:
Model architecture refers to the overall design of "how information flows and how to calculate" within the model. Just like the layout of a house: it can accommodate the same number of people, but the structure of two bedrooms and one living room and duplex is different, and the suitable residents and uses are also different. Different architectures are suitable for different tasks. The names Transformer, Diffusion Model, and MoE are actually "different approaches to the same type of things" and they all fall into the category of architecture.
Be careful not to mix three things together: architecture, model size, and model capabilities. Each is its own thing. Changing the architecture does not mean changing the model file. The former means that the design drawing has changed, while the latter means that the product has changed.
With the classification intuition of "architecture is a type of design method", if you encounter a string of "such and such models" later, you will be able to distinguish which ones are design methods and which ones are something else.

fields.精确定义: The core of a model architecture proposed in 2017 is to allow the model to "simultaneously pay attention to the relationship between all words" when processing a sentence. Therefore, it is particularly good at processing long texts and can become stronger by expanding the scale. Almost all big language models today are based on it.
fields.常见误解: Think of "Transformer" as a specific product name; or think that it is just a "faster neural network."
fields.典型案例: Explain "why the large model can understand the connection between the context and context in a sentence", but the early word-by-word processing method cannot.
fields.反例: Call any AI a Transformer.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "what problems it solves and why it is important" and does not talk about attention calculation formulas and matrix operations.
fields.教学类比: For example, when reading a sentence, you don't read word by word in order, but "scan the whole sentence at a glance and grasp the relationship of all the words at the same time."
fields.来源依据: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017)
fields.通俗解释:
A model architecture proposed in 2017, and almost all major language models today are built on it. What problem does it solve? The old-fashioned way of processing a sentence is to follow it word by word, and forget the previous part after reading it; Transformer allows the model to pay attention to the relationship between all words at the same time when processing a sentence, so it is particularly good at dealing with long texts, and it can continue to become stronger by expanding the scale.
It's like reading a sentence not word by word in order, but scanning the whole sentence at a glance, grasping the relationship of all words at the same time. This is the way it reads the text.
There are two misunderstandings in the name: it is not a specific product name, nor is it a "faster neural network". Similarly, don’t call any AI a Transformer. There are many image models and other architectures.

fields.精确定义: The working method of the large language model is to continuously predict "the most likely word (word element) that will appear next". If one is predicted, it will be connected to the next one, and then the next one will be predicted, and the complete answer will be spelled out word by word.
fields.常见误解: Think that the model is "thinking about the entire paragraph before outputting it"; or thinking that it is "retrieving standard answers".
fields.典型案例: Observe the process of AI's word-for-word output and understand "why it said the wrong thing seriously" (probability is similar, but the fact is not necessarily correct).
fields.反例: Think of "smoothly received" as "said correctly."
fields.深度上限: We only talk about the intuition of "word-by-word prediction" and do not talk about probability distribution, sampling parameters and training mechanisms.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Understanding this helps students understand: Fluency ≠ Correct, self-check.
fields.教学类比: It's like the "associate next word" function of the mobile phone input method, except that the range of associations is much larger and the sentences are much longer.
fields.通俗解释:
The way the large language model generates answers is a bit simple: it constantly predicts "the most likely word to appear next", picks up the word after it predicts one, then predicts the next one, and spells out the entire answer word by word. This is called autoregressive generation.
Like the association function of the mobile phone input method, you type a word and it pops up the next one. However, the range of association of the model is much larger, and the sentences to be connected are much longer. It is not about thinking up the entire paragraph and then pouring it out, nor is it searching for standard answers.
This also explains why it says the wrong thing seriously: it is picking words that are "probably similar", which may not be true in fact. Smooth reception does not mean correct speaking. Read the AI's answer and check this step.

fields.精确定义: The number of adjustable "knobs" inside the model is called parameters; the larger the number of parameters, the stronger the capability, but the higher the training and running costs, and the more difficult it is to deploy to small devices. The configurations (such as learning rhythm and model structure) set by humans before the start of training are called "hyperparameters", which are different from the parameters learned during training.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "the bigger the parameter is, the better"; ignoring task matching and cost.
fields.典型案例: Compare the trade-offs between "large cloud model" and "small mobile phone model" in terms of capabilities, speed, and cost.
fields.反例: Just look at the parameter rankings to select a model.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "the relationship between size, ability, and cost" and does not talk about the specific mathematical meaning of the parameters.
fields.教学类比: Like a car's displacement: The bigger it is, the more powerful it is, but it consumes more fuel and makes it harder to park in a small parking space.
fields.通俗解释:
The adjustable "knobs" inside the model are called parameters, and the total number of knobs is the parameter amount. The general rule is: the larger the number of parameters, the stronger the capability, but the higher the cost of training and operation, and the more difficult it is to install it on small devices such as mobile phones. The choice between large cloud models and small mobile phone models is a realistic version of this rule: one is powerful but expensive and slow, the other is light but has limited capabilities.
It's the same as the displacement of a car: a large displacement is usually powerful, but consumes fuel and makes it difficult to park in a small parking space.
Another word to distinguish: hyperparameters, which refers to the configuration set by people before the start of training, such as learning rhythm and model structure, are different from the parameters learned by oneself during training. Selecting a model only by looking at the parameter rankings and ignoring task matching and cost is a common bias.

fields.精确定义: A type of model architecture for generating images, videos and other content. The idea is to "start from a bunch of random noise, remove the noise step by step, and gradually reveal a clear picture." Most drawing and video drawing tools today are based on it.
fields.常见误解: Understand "diffusion" as "spreading the picture"; or confuse it with the generation method of language model.
fields.典型案例: Explain that "AI drawing is not a collage of material libraries, but a picture that is 'erased' from noise step by step."
fields.反例: It is believed that AI drawing is "put together from pictures found on the Internet."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the intuition of "denoising into images", but does not talk about the diffusion equation and training objectives.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Generating images involves copyright and authenticity, and needs to be linked to the concept of content security.
fields.教学类比: Like a piece of fogged glass, AI rubs it over and over again, slowly erasing a clear picture.
fields.通俗解释:
The principle of AI drawing is not to find pictures from the material library and put them together. The idea of ​​​​an architecture such as the diffusion model is: starting from a group of random noise, removing the noise step by step, and the picture gradually emerges until a clear picture is revealed. Most of today's drawing and video drawing tools use this approach.
Like a piece of glass covered with fog, AI wipes it over and over again, the fog recedes bit by bit, and the painting is revealed bit by bit.
The "diffusion" in the name should not be understood as "spreading the picture." It refers to this denoising generation method, which is not the same as the language model's generation method of jumping out word by word. In addition, AI-generated images involve copyright and authenticity, so be careful when viewing them.

fields.精确定义: An architecture that allows large models to "division and cooperate": There are multiple "expert" sub-modules inside the model, and only the most relevant few are called for each processing, thereby reducing operating overhead while maintaining large capabilities.
fields.常见误解: Think that MoE is "multiple AIs discussing together"; or think that it must not be as strong as the "all-in-one" model.
fields.典型案例: Explain "why some large models are very capable but not very slow in response" - because only a part of them is used at a time.
fields.反例: Understand "multi-experts" as "multiple agents meeting".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the intuition of "dividing labor and calling and saving costs", but does not talk about routing algorithms and gating mechanisms.
fields.教学类比: Like the division of departments in a large hospital: it is not necessary for all departments to receive patients at the same time. According to the patient's condition, only the most relevant experts are called.
fields.通俗解释:
The mixed expert model, or MoE for short, is an architecture that allows large models to divide labor and cooperate: there are multiple "expert" sub-modules inside the model. Each time processing comes, only the few most relevant to the current content are selected to work, and the rest rest. In this way, the overall capacity is maintained, but the operating overhead is reduced.
Why are some large models not weak in ability and slow in response? Here's the secret: use only part of the team at a time, not all of them.
It is like the sub-specialty consultation in a large hospital: it is not necessary for all departments to open at the same time. It is enough to call the most relevant experts according to the patient's condition. Don’t get caught up in two misunderstandings: MoE is not “multiple AIs discussing together”, nor is it “not using all the computing power, so it must be weak”.

fields.精确定义: Let the model write out the reasoning process step by step ("first...then...so...") instead of giving the answer directly. Writing it down in steps makes it perform better on math, logic, etc. tasks, and makes it easier to check which step it made a mistake in.
fields.常见误解: Think that the "written thinking process" is the real inner activity of the model; regard the steps shown as necessarily faithful to its internal calculations.
fields.典型案例: For an application question, the AI is required to "list the steps before answering" and compare the accuracy of the answer directly.
fields.反例: Take "the steps are very similar" as "the reasoning must be correct".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "step-by-step expression is helpful for reasoning and inspection", not how to implement it internally.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Tip: "The reasoning process displayed is not entirely equal to the real decision-making process" to avoid excessive trust.
fields.教学类比: For example, when doing math problems, you are required to "write the steps to solve the problem", not just fill in the answer.
fields.通俗解释:
Let the model not give out the answer directly when answering the question, but write out the process step by step: "First what, then what, then what". This practice is called thinking chain. After the steps are laid out, the model will perform better on tasks such as mathematics and logic, and it will be easier for people to see where it went wrong.
It's the same as doing math problems: you are required to write down the steps to solve the problem, not just fill in the answers. Once the steps are written, it will be clear at a glance where you are stuck.
But one thing must be made clear: the "thinking process" written by the model may not be its true inner activity. The steps shown are not necessarily faithful to the internal calculations, and "the steps are written very similar" does not mean "the reasoning must be correct." You can watch its process, but don’t believe it entirely.

fields.精确定义: It means that after the scale of the model increases to a certain extent, it suddenly shows abilities that the small model does not have (such as multi-step reasoning). It is called emergent abilities in English; the phenomenon of "ability suddenly getting better" that occurs during training is often called "Aha Moment".
fields.常见误解: It is believed that "ability grows gradually and linearly"; or "emergence" is regarded as metaphysics and cannot be explained.
fields.典型案例: Compare the performance difference between small models and large models for the same task, and understand "quantitative change to qualitative change".
fields.反例: Use "emergence" to explain all incomprehensible phenomena.
fields.深度上限: We only talk about the phenomenon that "new capabilities will emerge when the scale reaches a certain level", and do not talk about the details of the methodological debate on whether it actually exists.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Reminder: Emergent capabilities also come with new unpredictable risks.
fields.教学类比: For example, water does not boil until it is heated to 100°C - no change was visible even after adding many degrees before.
fields.来源依据: Wei et al., Emergent Abilities of LLMs (2022)
fields.通俗解释:
As the model gets bigger, its capabilities get stronger, but it doesn't grow at a uniform rate. There is a phenomenon: after the scale increases to a certain extent, capabilities that are completely lacking in small models suddenly appear, such as multi-step reasoning. This is called emergent capability. The moment when "ability suddenly improves" during training is often called the epiphany moment.
Just like boiling water, no movement can be seen all the way through the heating, and it will boil as soon as it reaches 100°C. Those degrees that were added before were not in vain, they were just saved, and they only appeared after enough points were saved.
Don’t think of the growth of capabilities as a straight line rising at a constant speed, and don’t use “emergence” as a slogan to explain everything, stuffing in all the phenomena you don’t understand. There is another layer of reminder: the new capabilities that emerge also bring new and unpredictable risks.

3-27.name: Reward Model and Preference Optimization Family

fields.精确定义: In order to make AI's answers "more in line with human preferences", first train a "scorer" (reward model) with human/AI preferences, and then use it to guide model improvement. RLHF, DPO, GRPO, and RLVR are all different practices in this family, each with its own emphasis.
fields.常见误解: Think that "the model knows what is right and wrong"; ignore the bias that may be introduced in the preference data.
fields.典型案例: Explain "why different versions of the same model have different answer styles" - behind this is the role of preference training.
fields.反例: Think of "catering to users" as "more correct".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the intuition and family relationship of "using scoring to guide the model to become better", and does not talk about the formula details of each algorithm.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Preferences come from people and therefore inherit biases; reminder that "pleasing" does not equal "correct".
fields.教学类比: Just like when a teacher grades an essay, the students change their writing style according to the tendency of the scoring - if the score is biased, the writing style will also be biased.
fields.通俗解释:
To make AI's answers more satisfactory to humans, the method is to first train a "scorer": use the preference data given by humans or AI to teach it to score the answers, and then use this score to guide model improvement. This scorer is called a reward model. RLHF, DPO, GRPO, and RLVR are all different approaches in this family. Each approach has its own focus, but the core is the same: using scoring to guide the model to become better.
Why are the answering styles so different in different versions of the same model? Preference training is often at work behind this.
It's like a teacher grading a composition: the student will change the writing style according to the grader's taste. If the grade is biased, the writing style will also be biased. So don’t think that “the model knows right and wrong on its own”. Its “views of right and wrong” are fed into it, and the biases in the preference data will be learned along with it. It’s also important to understand: Just because the answer is what you want does not mean it is more correct.

fields.精确定义: After the model training is completed, the process of calculating output and generating answers for new inputs using fixed parameters is called inference - it is also often called "inference" in daily life, which is the industry meaning of "run once" of the model. Note the distinction: the "reasoning" of the inference model is reasoning (multi-step thinking before answering), which is not the same thing as "running once" inference; "expending more computing power to think when answering difficult questions" belongs to the calculation method in the inference stage (see 3-17 Scaling Law).
fields.常见误解: Confusing the reasoning of "inference model" with the inference of running the model once; understanding "reasoning" only as logical reasoning; confusing training and inference.
fields.典型案例: Distinguish between "it takes several months to train a large model" and "it only takes a few seconds to answer a question"; the ordinary model answers directly, and the inference model will first output a "thinking process" before giving the answer.
fields.反例: Think of "an updated version of the model" and "the model is answering you" as the same thing.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the distinction between terminology and training/use, but not about inference optimization technology.
fields.教学类比: For example, answering questions in exams (inference) and writing a draft before answering the question ("thinking" of the inference model) - writing a longer draft may not necessarily make it faster, but the problem will be more stable.
fields.通俗解释:
The word "reasoning" refers to two different things in the AI circle, which must be separated. One is inference: after the model training is completed, the parameters are fixed, the new input is calculated and an answer is given. This is often called "inference" in daily life. This is what the industry calls "one run". The other thing is the "reasoning" of the reasoning model: generate a multi-step thinking before answering, and use more calculations in exchange for accuracy on complex tasks. Two different things.
Take an exam as an analogy: answering questions and handing them in is inference, drafting and listing steps before answering questions is the "thinking" of the reasoning model. Longer drafts are not necessarily faster, but they are more stable on difficult issues.
Don’t mix up the stages: it takes several months to train a large model, but it only takes a few seconds to answer a question. The former is training, and the latter is use. The ordinary model answers directly, while the reasoning model will spit out a thinking process before giving the answer. This is the most intuitive difference between the two.

fields.精确定义: A set of standardized questions (benchmark) is used to compare the capabilities of different models, and rankings are given like test scores. Benchmarks can reflect some abilities, but they may be "tested" after the questions are made public, and they cannot fully represent real usability.
fields.常见误解: Use the list ranking as the only criterion for the quality of the model; ignore the difference between the benchmark and the real usage scenario.
fields.典型案例: Look at a model list, discuss "whether a high score equals ease of use", and cite important factors outside the list.
fields.反例: Just look at the scores and draw conclusions.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "what the benchmark is, what it can explain, and what it cannot explain", and does not talk about the specific evaluation methodology.
fields.安全与伦理边界: We are reminded that the list may be commercially exploited, and we need to be wary of "swiping the list".
fields.教学类比: Like test scores: they can explain some levels, but one score cannot explain the whole person.
fields.来源依据: Popular benchmarks such as LMSYS Arena / MMLU
fields.通俗解释:
Comparing the levels of different models relies on a benchmark: a set of standardized questions, just like an exam. Each model takes the same paper and ranks them according to their scores. Scores can reflect part of ability, and this "report card" is indeed useful.
But one score cannot describe the whole person. The benchmark questions are open to the public. If you do so, you may be "tested". If you practice specifically according to the question types, your score will go up, but your real ability may not be able to keep up. There is a gap between the rankings on the list and the actual usage scenarios.
So don’t use the list ranking as the only criterion for judging the quality of a model, and don’t draw conclusions just by looking at the running scores. There is an extra layer of caution: the list may be commercially exploited, and "list-swiping" is a real thing.

fields.精确定义: It refers to the system used by the platform to "guess what you like to watch": it predicts what you might like next based on your past behavior (what you clicked, how long you watched it, what you bought), and then recommends it to you. It’s all behind the endless viewing of short videos, the “guessing” of shopping, and the more accurate the music list becomes. It is the end of the chain of "classifier-predictor-recommender".
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "recommendations are random" or "what was recommended to me is what I really need"; ignoring that it is designed to prolong your stay.
fields.典型案例: Compare the difference in recommended content between a new account and an old account, and understand "why recommendations require getting to know you first."
fields.反例: Think of "popular recommendations" as "the real choice of most people."
fields.深度上限: We only talk about the intuition of the mechanism of "predicting your preferences based on your behavior" and do not talk about algorithm details such as collaborative filtering.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Linking to the "information cocoon" (2-17) and the "attention economy" (6-24) is the mechanism chain for understanding "how AI affects me".
fields.教学类比: Like a store clerk who is familiar with you, if you look at the product twice, he will remember it and take the initiative to show it to you next time.
fields.通俗解释:
Why can’t I stop short videos after swiping them? Why can shopping software always “guess” you? Why does the music list become more familiar the more you listen to it? Behind the scenes is a recommendation system: the platform predicts what you might like next based on your past behavior, what you clicked on, how long you looked at it, and what you bought, and then recommends it to you. It stands at the end of the chain of "classifier, predictor, and recommender".
It's like a store clerk who knows you well: if you look at the products twice, he silently notes them and puts them in front of you next time. The content displayed by the new account is much different from that of the old account. This is because the old account has thicker behavior records and is easier to guess.
Two sentences to keep in mind: recommendations are not randomly distributed, but "recommended to me" does not mean "what I really need". This system was originally designed to extend your stay. It is connected to the information cocoon and the attention economy. Only by understanding it can you understand how AI affects you.

fields.精确定义: It refers to a learning method of "learning by trial and error": the machine keeps trying and adjusts its methods according to the results. If it does it right, it will strengthen it, and if it does it wrong, it will correct it. It is the representative technology of behaviorism among the three major schools of AI. The "self-playing" used by AlphaGo is its advanced gameplay - playing chess by yourself, without human guidance, and figuring out by yourself by winning or losing. This is a completely different learning method from the large language model "reading massive texts to learn rules" (belonging to connectionism).
fields.常见误解: Confusing reinforcement learning with "supervised learning" (one relies on trial and error feedback, the other relies on standard answers); thinking that there is only one way for AI to learn.
fields.典型案例: Compare "AlphaGo, which learns chess by playing against itself" and "ChatGPT, which learns to speak by reading text" to understand the difference between the two learning methods.
fields.反例: I think "AI learns everything by feeding it data."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the intuition of "learning from trial and error and self-playing", and does not talk about the details of the reward function and algorithm.
fields.教学类比: It's like learning to ride a bicycle: no one will give you a standard answer. Just fall a few times and adjust a few times, and you will slowly find a sense of balance.
fields.来源依据: General concepts of reinforcement learning (Sutton & Barto); AlphaGo self-play; gaps named by users
fields.通俗解释:
There is a way of learning that does not rely on textbooks: the machine keeps trying on its own, adjusts its approach based on the results, strengthens what it does right, corrects what it does wrong, and slowly finds its way out. This is reinforcement learning, the representative technology of behaviorism among the three major schools of AI. Its advanced gameplay is called self-play: you play chess with yourself, without human guidance, and you rely on yourself to win or lose. This is how AlphaGo was trained.
It's like learning to ride a bicycle: no one can give you a "standard answer". Just fall a few times, adjust a few times, and the feeling of balance will grow on its own.
It has two approaches to learning large language models: one learns from trial and error and winning and losing, and the other learns rules by reading massive texts. "AI learns everything by feeding it data" is not accurate, there is more than one way to learn. Don’t confuse it with supervised learning that “learns from standard answers”. One relies on trial and error feedback, and the other relies on answer comparison.

fields.精确定义: It means that AI can predict "unknown results" based on "known clues" - such as predicting what three-dimensional structure a protein will fold into based on the sequence of a string of amino acids. It relies on learning patterns from a large number of known "structural samples". The ability to "predict structure" represents an important use of AI in scientific research.
fields.常见误解: Think that "AI is for experimentation"; ignore that it is currently mainly about "prediction and calculation", and experimentation and verification still rely on humans.
fields.典型案例: Understand the process of "giving AI a string of amino acids and it predicts the three-dimensional structure" and discuss why it can help biologists.
fields.反例: I thought that "the structure predicted by AI must be correct and there is no need to verify it."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the intuition of "predicting unknown results from known clues" and does not talk about protein folding and model network structure.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Scientific conclusions still need to be verified experimentally, and AI is a tool, not an authority.
fields.教学类比: Just like looking at a person's handwriting, you can guess what he or she looks like - it's a rule that you've learned from seeing many examples.
fields.来源依据: AlphaFold2 A popular expression of the structure prediction principle; a gap named by the user
fields.通俗解释:
One of the major uses of AI in scientific research is to "predict unknown results from known clues." Typical scenario: Given the sequence of a string of amino acids to AI, it predicts the shape of this chain after folding into a three-dimensional form. It relies on learning a large number of known structural samples first, summarizing the rules from them, and then using the rules to infer unseen ones.
Just like looking at a person's handwriting, you can guess what he or she looks like. It's not magic, it's just seeing too many examples and summarizing the corresponding relationship. Such predictions can be of great help to biologists trying to figure out protein structures.
Two boundaries are drawn: AI does not do experiments for people, it mainly does predictions and calculations, and experiments and verification still rely on people; the structures it predicts are not guaranteed to be correct, and scientific conclusions must ultimately be tested by experiments. AI is a tool, not an authority.

fields.精确定义: Large models that can simultaneously receive and process text, images, audio, video and other modal inputs, and some can natively output multiple modalities.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
Ordinary large models mainly recognize text, while the "multiple" of multi-modal large models means that it can receive multiple forms of input at the same time: text, images, audio, and video, all of which can be processed together. Some can also go the other way and output several modes natively.
This is how people receive information: watching, listening, and reading. The large multi-modal model goes in the same direction, merging several channels together instead of managing each channel separately.
You can think of it as a model with "open eyes, ears, and mouth": in the past, you could only "read", but now you can also "see" and "listen", and some can also "speak" and "draw". The way the model receives and expresses information is therefore much wider.

fields.精确定义: A type of large model that grows the internal reasoning process of the chain (thinking chain) before answering the question, using more reasoning stage calculations in exchange for accuracy in complex tasks. Note: "Reasoning" here refers to reasoning (multi-step thinking), which is not the same thing as "inference" (see 3-28) in the model use stage.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.来源依据: OpenAI“Learning to Reason with LLMs”；DeepSeek-R1, arXiv:2501.12948
fields.通俗解释:
There is a type of large model that requires a long internal reasoning process before answering, and you must think it through step by step before answering. This type of model is called an inference model. The extra "thinking" it spends results in higher accuracy on complex tasks.
The "reasoning" here refers to multi-step thinking, which is not the same as the "run once" inference during the model use stage. The two words look similar in Chinese, but have different meanings.
The intuitive difference between it and the ordinary model is that after you ask a question, the ordinary model directly gives the answer, while the inference model will first spit out a thinking process and then fall on the answer. The price is that you have to spend more calculations before answering, and the accuracy in exchange for difficult questions is more valuable.

fields.精确定义: Use the output of the large model (teacher model) to train the small model (student model) to improve the ability of the small model to that of the large model.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
Model distillation is a method of "teaching a large model to a small one": using the output of a large model (teacher model) to train a small model (student model), bringing the student's ability up to a level close to that of a teacher. What students learn is the output given by the large model, rather than learning from scratch.
Just like a teacher does not let students chew textbooks, but tells students the lectures he has digested, students' starting point is much higher than trying to figure it out on their own.
The terms "teacher" and "student" refer to the relationship between the two models, the big one and the small one: the big one outputs it as a teaching material, and the small one learns from it and develops their skills. Note that what students learn is the teacher’s output, not directly moving the teacher’s files over and renaming them.

fields.精确定义: Use the evaluation/preference given by the AI model to replace part of the human annotation as a reinforcement learning reward signal.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
Training an AI requires evaluating signals: which answers are good and which are bad. RLAIF's approach is to let the AI ​​model act as the evaluator: use the evaluation or preference given by the AI ​​to replace part of the manual annotation as a reward signal in reinforcement learning.
There is only one core difference between it and the method of "scoring by people": the one who scores is replaced by a model. The name is directly readable, RL is reinforcement learning, and AIF is feedback from AI. Together they are "AI feedback reinforcement learning".
Be aware: the evaluator itself is also an AI, and its evaluation will be imparted to the trained model along with the reward signal. The quality of evaluation directly determines the direction in which training will go.

fields.精确定义: All further training of the model after the pre-training is completed, including fine-tuning, alignment, reasoning ability enhancement, etc.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
The training of a large model is not completed at once. There is a long period of pre-training first: reading massive data and developing basic abilities. All further training after this is collectively referred to as post-training: fine-tuning, alignment, and strengthening of reasoning abilities are all counted in this stage.
You can use the analogy of learning to drive: pre-training is like practicing basic skills in a driving school, and post-training is like targeted exercises after getting a driver's license, specializing in a certain event and honing difficult movements, so that people can change from "being able to drive" to "driving well".
The location is easy to remember: all training that occurs after pre-training is placed in the post-training basket. Pre-training lays the foundation, and post-training does further processing. The two steps are connected to form a complete training process.

fields.精确定义: Learn internal representation models of how the environment changes over time and predict the consequences of actions for planning and agent training.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
The world model is a set of representations of "how the world works" learned inside the model: it learns how the environment changes over time and can also predict the consequences of a certain action.
There are two main uses: one is for planning, where you need to internally deduce a few steps before taking action to see which path will work; the other is for intelligent agent training, which serves as a "training ground" for it.
It's like a chess player mentally arranging a chess game: he doesn't need to actually make a move, he first thinks in his mind, "If I make this move, the opponent will probably make that move," and then make a decision after deducing it for a few rounds. The world model is the machine's "mental chess game" draft. After all, the manuscript is a learned representation, not the same thing as the real world.

fields.精确定义: Technology that makes the AI decision-making process and basis understandable to humans, including explanation of the internal mechanism of the model and description of the output basis.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
AI gives a conclusion, but humans can’t see how it came to it. What interpretability technology wants to solve is this “incomprehensibility”: making AI’s decision-making process and basis understandable to humans.
It contains two parts: one is to look inward and explain how the internal mechanism of the model works; the other is to look out and explain why a certain output is given.
Just like a doctor seeing a doctor, he cannot just prescribe medicine. He must also provide the basis for diagnosis, which indicators and symptoms support the judgment. Explainability is to equip AI with the ability to "explain the basis". If you can't explain why you draw a conclusion, you will always feel unsure when using it; only if you can explain it, others will be able to check its conclusion.

fields.精确定义: AI drives physical entities such as robots to perceive and act in the real world.
