This article talks about: recognize the rights and interests involved, keep the boundaries, leave the decision-making power to others, and be responsible for the results of use and release.
There are two ideas that need to be discarded: one is "it was generated by AI, so if something goes wrong, it's not mine", and the other is "I marked it as AI, so I'm exempt from liability." Labeling is honesty, not shielding.
It's like using a calculator to do accounting - if the calculation is wrong, the person doing the accounting will be the one to apologize, and the calculator will not pay for you. There is a practical self-examination method. Before publishing, ask five questions: Where does the data come from? Who checked? Who is affected? Who decides? Do you want to publish it? If you can answer the five questions and answers, then consider publishing them; if you can't answer them, it's not time yet.

fields.精确定义: The systems, norms, supervision and responsibility arrangements established around the development and use of AI.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstanding is that "governance is only the government's business" (enterprises, schools and users are all involved).
fields.典型案例: The platform requires identification of AI-generated content; school classes formulate AI usage agreements.
fields.反例: Thinking that "there are no rules so you can use it casually".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "having rules and responsible arrangements" and does not talk about the details of policy provisions and macro-system analysis.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Students only learn the rules and boundaries related to their own use.
fields.来源依据: NIST AI RMF (Govern/Map/Measure/Manage); China’s “Interim Measures for Generative Artificial Intelligence Service Management” (2023)
fields.通俗解释:
The government is doing this, as are businesses, schools, and every user in setting rules for AI. AI governance refers to the systems, norms, supervision and responsibility arrangements established around the development and use of AI.
It looks a bit like traffic rules: traffic lights are set by the traffic control department, drivers obey traffic rules, pedestrians also have their own walking patterns, and a community can also set its own parking rules. Correspondingly, the platform requires that the content generated by AI be marked, which is the platform's specification; schools and classes formulate AI usage agreements, which are the rules of the campus; when you use AI, abiding by the agreement is part of governance.
There are two misunderstandings that need to be clarified: one is that "governance is only a matter for the government", but in fact all parties are involved; the other is that "if there are no rules, you can use them casually" - just because there are no rules in sight does not mean that there is no need to abide by the rules.

fields.精确定义: The impact of AI on job structure, skill demand and employment distribution, as well as the environmental impact of electricity, water resources and carbon emissions consumed by training and operating AI; future choices refer to value judgments made in the human-machine relationship.
fields.常见误解: The misunderstandings are that "AI will inevitably lead to large-scale unemployment"; "AI only affects low-skilled jobs"; "Energy consumption for each AI query is fixed."
fields.典型案例: Discuss "which jobs will be replaced and which ones will be done better with AI."
fields.反例: Use a threatening narrative to render “AI replaces everything”.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about labor and environmental impacts related to students’ lives, and does not extend to macro-policy and professional ethics courses.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Threatening future narratives and promises of ability without effort are prohibited (Master Edition §8.2 Red Link).
fields.来源依据: IEA "Energy and AI"; Master §3.1 K6 "Labor and Environmental Impact"
fields.通俗解释:
AI changes more than just “who does the work.” It affects the job structure, skill requirements and employment distribution: some jobs will be replaced, and other jobs can be done better by AI. At the same time, AI itself is also a "big energy consumer" - training and operation consume electricity, water resources, and produce carbon emissions. It's like adding a very capable machine to your home: the work assignments have changed, and the water and electricity bills have also increased. How to choose in the face of these changes is called future choice, which refers to the value judgment made in the human-machine relationship.
Several assertions are untenable: "AI will inevitably lead to large-scale unemployment," "AI only affects low-skilled jobs," and "the energy consumption of each AI query is fixed." These statements are too absolute. To use a threatening narrative to describe "AI replacing everything" is to take the discussion astray.
A more reliable way to ask is to be more specific: Which aspects of this work will be replaced? In which areas can people do better with AI?

fields.精确定义: It refers to the risks posed by “AI itself may be uncontrollable, difficult to understand, or even deviate from human intentions” and how humans maintain dominance over it. It is different from "someone maliciously attacks AI" (technical security). It focuses on the social risks brought by the system itself.
fields.常见误解: Understand "AI security" only as "anti-hacker"; or replace the discussion of real risks with a sci-fi-style narrative of out-of-control.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "How can humans maintain control if AI's capabilities grow faster than we can understand it", distinguishing real topics from science fiction imagination.
fields.反例: Treat "AI is very good" as "certainly safe".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "why controllability is a problem and what are the practical concerns" and does not develop technical alignment methods.
fields.安全与伦理边界: This section is the backbone of ethics and civilization issues and must be based on facts and avoid panic.
fields.教学类比: It's like raising a bulldog that gets smarter and more powerful: it's not that it's bad, it's that you have to keep the leash at all times.
fields.通俗解释:
When discussing AI security, many people’s first reaction is to prevent hackers and viruses, but this article talks about another story: AI itself may be uncontrollable, difficult to understand, and even deviate from human intentions. This is a social risk brought by the system itself, and the technical security of "someone maliciously attacks AI" are two issues. What humans have to worry about is: how to always hold the leadership.
Dog owners understand this: a bulldog that grows bigger and stronger is not bad, but you must always hold the leash. If the rope is loose, the greater the strength, the more dangerous it will be.
Both extremes should be avoided: one is to use the words "anti-hacker" to summarize AI security; the other is to use science fiction-style out-of-control narratives to replace the discussion of real risks. "AI is very good" does not mean "it must be safe". The question worthy of serious discussion is this: If AI capabilities grow faster than we can understand it, how can humans maintain control?

fields.精确定义: [This section is an extended concept of 6-11 AI safety and controllability] refers to the problem of "how to solve the problem of how to make smarter systems obey humans before the emergence of super intelligence." It assumes that once AI becomes smarter than humans, it may not be enough to use human supervision to manage it, so it is necessary to study in advance the method of "using small abilities to manage large abilities".
fields.常见误解: Think of "super alignment" as a solved technology; or think of "just set the rules."
fields.典型案例: Discuss "How does the teacher make sure you follow the rules when you know more than the invigilator?" by analogy with the alignment problem.
fields.反例: It is thought that super intelligence can be restrained by "writing rules into the program".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "what the problem is and why it is difficult" and does not talk about research routes and technical solutions.
fields.安全与伦理边界: It belongs to a value discussion and avoids assertions and panic.
fields.教学类比: For example, asking primary school students to check the homework of university professors - how to control if their abilities are not equal?
fields.来源依据: Popular discussions on projects such as OpenAI Superalignment
fields.通俗解释:
If one day AI becomes smarter than humans, will humans still be able to control it? This is what Super Alignment asks: before the emergence of super intelligence, first solve the problem of "how to make smarter systems obey humans." There is a hypothesis behind it: Once AI is smarter than humans, it may not be enough to rely on humans to supervise it, so we must study in advance the method of "using small capabilities to manage large capabilities".
What's the problem? It's like asking primary school students to check the homework of university professors - the abilities are not equal, and the one who is checking is weaker. How to check? If you know more than the invigilator, how can the teacher ensure that you obey the rules? If you can't understand these two issues, you won't understand the difficulty of alignment.
There are two misunderstandings to avoid: one is to regard it as a solved technology, and the other is to think that "just write the rules into the program and everything will be fine." It is still an unsolved problem.

fields.精确定义: It refers to making AI behave in line with human values, but "whose values" and "which culture is right and wrong" are themselves controversial issues. Value alignment is not just a technical issue, but also a matter of ethical and social choice.
fields.常见误解: Believing that "values are unique and self-evident"; ignoring differences between different cultures and groups.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "should the answers given to the same question be the same in different regions" and understand the differences in value.
fields.反例: Treat the preferences of a certain group as the consensus of all mankind.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the problem awareness of "diversity of values and trade-offs in alignment" and does not talk about the alignment algorithm.
fields.安全与伦理边界: This book is the core of ethical discussions and must present multiple positions and not regard a single position as a technical conclusion (Master Edition §8.2).
fields.教学类比: It's like setting laws for a country: what to set and who has the final say is the biggest controversy in itself.
fields.通俗解释:
Let AI behave in line with human values - it sounds natural, but the trouble lies precisely in the words "human values": who has the final say? In which culture does right and wrong count? These issues alone cannot lead to consensus. Therefore, value alignment is not just a technical issue, it is also an ethical issue and a social choice issue.
It's like setting laws for a country: what laws to make and who to make them is the biggest controversy in itself. The same goes for AI. Should the answers to the same question be the same in different regions? If you think about this question, you can feel the difference in value.
There is a tacit thought that needs to be relaxed: values ​​are not unique and self-evident, and there are real differences between different cultures and different groups. This pitfall must be avoided by treating the preferences of a certain group as the consensus of all mankind.

fields.精确定义: Refers to the long-term relationship between humans and increasingly powerful AI living, working, and creating: Is AI a tool, a partner, or a competitor? Will people's roles in this relationship be redefined? This is a long-term issue related to the direction of civilization.
fields.常见误解: Falling into the extreme narrative of "AI replacing humans"; or being blindly optimistic and believing that "technology will naturally improve."
fields.典型案例: Discuss "When AI can participate in creation and decision-making, where will the irreplaceable value of human beings be reflected?"
fields.反例: Replace specific discussions with simple conclusions of "humanity will win/humanity will lose."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the "core issues in the symbiotic relationship" and does not make predictions or assertions.
fields.安全与伦理边界: The core issues you named. Students must be guided to form a well-founded and multi-faceted stance.
fields.教学类比: Just like the relationship between humans and fire - fire can keep you warm or burn down your house. The key lies in how people get along with it.
fields.通俗解释:
Humans and increasingly capable AI will live, work, and create together for a long time. What exactly is AI in this relationship: a tool? partner? competitor? Will people's role be redefined? This is what needs to be discussed about the symbiosis and coexistence of human civilization and AI. It is a long-term issue related to the direction of civilization.
The relationship between ancestors and fire can be used as a comparison: fire can keep people warm, and it can also burn down the house. The key to how well one lives depends on how one gets along with it. The same is true for AI. The way you get along is more important than the machine itself.
Both narratives are unreliable: one is the extreme scaremongering of "AI replacing humans", the other is blind optimism and the belief that "technology will naturally get better." One-sentence conclusions such as "mankind will win" or "mankind will lose" cannot replace concrete discussions. The real question worth thinking about is: When AI can participate in creation and decision-making, what is the irreplaceable value of humans?

fields.精确定义: When AI can also write, paint, accompany, and comfort people, how will it affect people's uniqueness, creativity, and meaning of existence? This issue is about human dignity - not "can people beat AI", but "what do people want to be".
fields.常见误解: Use "efficiency" to judge the value of people; or equate "AI can do it" with "human efforts are meaningless".
fields.典型案例: Discuss "If AI can also write poetry, does it make sense for humans to write poetry?" and appreciate the value of the process.
fields.反例: Treat "AI can do it better" as "people shouldn't do it anymore".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the problem awareness of "meaning and dignity" and does not make philosophical conclusions.
fields.安全与伦理边界: The core issues you named. Encourage students to express their true confusion without imposing values.
fields.教学类比: Just like the advent of the camera, painting has not disappeared, but has taken a new direction.
fields.通俗解释:
AI can write poems, so what’s the use of people writing poems? Behind this question is a whole issue: when AI can also write, paint, accompany, and comfort people, how will it affect people's uniqueness, creativity, and meaning of existence? Its focus is not on "whether people can beat AI", but on "what people want to be" - this is about human dignity.
When the camera appeared, painting did not die, but found a new path. The relationship between AI and people can also draw some reference from this incident: the emergence of a new tool often forces people to rethink the meaning of what they do.
There are two algorithms that need to be thrown away: one is to judge the value of people based on their efficiency, because people are not efficient machines; the other is "AI can do it, so human efforts are meaningless." AI does a better job, but that doesn’t mean people should stop doing it. The process of doing things has value in itself. This question cannot be solved hastily with the word “efficiency”.

fields.精确定义: It refers to protecting minors in an environment where AI is popular: preventing addiction, preventing exposure to harmful content, preventing excessive collection of personal privacy, and preventing being misled by false information generated by AI. This is the shared responsibility of society.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that “AI content is naturally suitable for children”; ignoring the potential impact of recommendation algorithms and companion AI on growth.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "Is companion AI a good thing or a hidden danger for children?" and weigh the convenience and risks.
fields.反例: Think of "parental controls" as the only solution.
fields.深度上限: We only talk about the key points of protection related to ourselves, not the details of policy provisions.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Involves multiple responsibilities of guardianship, platform and individuals.
fields.教学类比: Be especially careful when giving medication to children - the same thing affects people of different ages differently.
fields.来源依据: China's "Regulations on the Internet Protection of Minors", etc.
fields.通俗解释:
Using the same AI, adults and children have different things to worry about. The protection of minors is about protecting children in an environment where AI is popular: preventing addiction, preventing exposure to harmful content, preventing excessive collection of personal privacy, and preventing being misled by false information generated by AI. This is the common responsibility of the whole society.
The caution in using medicines for children can be borrowed: the same medicine is fine for adults, but children must reduce the dosage and use it with caution. The same goes for AI. It is not naturally suitable for children. We cannot pretend to be blind to where the recommendation algorithm guides children and the potential impact of companion AI on children’s growth.
Don’t go to the two extremes: one is that “AI content is naturally harmless and can be used casually”, and the other is to regard “parental monitoring” as the only solution. Convenience and risk must be weighed together to be accurate.

fields.精确定义: AI will change the job structure: some repetitive tasks will be replaced, and new requirements will arise for "people who can use AI to do better". It may also give rise to new professions (new positions such as prompt engineering and AI application engineering have appeared in recent years). It affects not only "whether there is a job", but also the way of working and social division of labor.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that “AI will only grab low-skilled jobs”; or concluding that “a certain profession will definitely disappear”.
fields.典型案例: Analyze “which aspects of a specific occupation will be taken over by AI and which areas require more people.”
fields.反例: Replace concrete analysis with a scare narrative of “AI taking over jobs.”
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "structural changes and personal responses" and does not make macro predictions.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Avoid scaremongering future narratives (master §8.2 red line).
fields.教学类比: For example, after the advent of ATMs, tellers did not disappear, but their work content changed.
fields.通俗解释:
After the advent of ATMs, bank tellers did not disappear, but their jobs changed. The employment changes brought about by AI also follow the same logic: some repetitive jobs are replaced, and new requirements emerge for "people who can use AI to do better jobs." This may also give rise to a whole new profession - prompt engineering and AI application engineering that have appeared in recent years are such new positions.
It affects not only the matter of "whether there is a job," but also the way of working and the social division of labor itself. Therefore, when judging the prospects of a profession, don’t ask “will it disappear?”, but break it down and look at: In this profession, which links will be taken over by AI, and which links require more people?
Both statements are too crude: "AI will only grab low-skilled jobs", or conclude that "a certain occupation will definitely disappear." The intimidating narrative of “AI stealing jobs” also cannot replace specific analysis.

fields.精确定义: It refers to the gap between different regions and groups in their abilities and opportunities to use AI: schools with conditions and schools without conditions, people who can use it and people who cannot use it. The gap may be amplified by AI. How to make AI a force to narrow the gap is an important social issue.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "AI will automatically benefit everyone"; ignoring the differences in access thresholds and usage capabilities.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "Does AI make education fairer or less fair?" and give positive and negative examples.
fields.反例: Think of "having tools" as "it's only fair".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "expression and intuition of causes of gaps" and does not talk about macro policies.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Guide students to see the dual possibilities of technological inclusion and inequality.
fields.教学类比: Just like when the Internet first became popular—some people were already online, and some were not yet connected to electricity.
fields.通俗解释:
When the Internet first became popular, some places already had access to the Internet, and some places did not have electricity yet. The AI ​​​​era is also a similar situation: there is a gap in the ability and opportunities to use AI in different regions and different groups - schools with conditions and schools without conditions, those who can use it and those who cannot use it are not even close to each other.
The trouble is that this gap may be further amplified by AI: those who can use it can run faster with AI, while those who can't use it will be further behind. Letting AI become a force that narrows the gap, rather than widens it, is an important social issue.
There are two assumptions that need to be debunked: first, "AI will automatically benefit everyone." Whether the benefits are automatic depends on the acquisition threshold and ability to use them; second, "it is fair if you have the tools." There is a big gap between having the tools and actually using them well.

fields.精确定义: Faced with increasingly powerful AI, humans have to make a series of choices: enhance humans or constrain technology? Who has control? How to distribute the value created by AI? There are no standard answers to these choices, but each generation needs to make judgments based on facts and values.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "the future is automatically determined by technology and has nothing to do with people"; or giving up thinking and going with the flow.
fields.典型案例: Organize a debate: "What should humans protect most in the AI era?" and ask for reasons and evidence.
fields.反例: Treat "technological optimism" or "technological pessimism" as the only correct answers.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about "the existence and basis of choice", without making any conclusions or creating panic.
fields.安全与伦理边界: This book is the closing point of the whole value discussion and must present multiple positions.
fields.教学类比: It's like standing at a crossroads: each road leads to a different future, and the choice is in people's hands.
fields.通俗解释:
Standing at a crossroads, each road leads to a different future - facing increasingly capable AI, humans are standing at such a crossroads and have to make a series of choices: Should we enhance humans or limit technology? Who has control? How is the value created by AI distributed? There are no standard answers to these questions, but each generation has to make its own judgments based on facts and values.
The key is to get rid of the idea that the future is automatically determined by technology and has nothing to do with people. Technology does not choose its own path, people do. Another pitfall to avoid is to give up thinking, go with the flow, and regard "technological optimism" or "technological pessimism" as the only correct stance.
When it's time to take a stand, learn the rules of debate: give your reasons and present your evidence. For example, in the debate topic: "In the era of AI, what should human beings protect most?" Whoever claims it will give evidence.

fields.精确定义: In China, algorithms that provide AI services to the public need to register with the competent authorities, describing what it does, what risks it may have, and who is responsible. This is an institutional arrangement where "AI services must be managed by someone."
fields.常见误解: They think that "algorithms are technologies and should not be controlled"; or they think that filing means security.
fields.典型案例: Understand "why the cyberspace department requires platforms to explain the use of algorithms" and understand the basic logic of governance.
fields.反例: Thinking that "there is no need to go through any formalities to launch an AI application".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the common sense that "there is a filing system and the purpose is to manage responsibilities" and does not talk about the details of the declaration process.
fields.安全与伦理边界: The governance system is the guarantee for the implementation of responsibilities and forms a supporting system with individual responsibilities.
fields.教学类比: For example, when opening a store, you need a business license: it’s not that you don’t trust you, but you have to find someone if something goes wrong.
fields.来源依据: China's "Internet Information Service Algorithm Recommendation Management Regulations" etc.
fields.通俗解释:
To open a store, you need to apply for a business license and provide AI services to the public. There are also similar procedures: algorithm filing. In China, algorithms that provide AI services to the public need to register with the competent authorities and clearly explain what they do, what risks they may have, and who will be responsible if something goes wrong.
The purpose of this arrangement is not difficult to understand: if something happens, someone needs to be found. The platform is required to explain the purpose of the algorithm, which is how this system works - not to distrust anyone, but to have a name that clearly states responsibility behind each service.
Two misunderstandings need to be corrected: first, "algorithms are technologies and should not be managed." The more popular the technology is, the more people need to be in charge; second, "registration means safety." Registration is responsibility registration, not safety certification. Don’t say “there are no procedures required to launch an AI application”, there are procedures.

fields.精确定义: This is a popular saying in the industry, not a strict technical definition: "hard distillation" refers to directly copying the output of other people's models to train your own model, which is close to plagiarism in nature; "soft distillation" refers to learning other people's ideas, methods and abilities, and then combining your own innovation to make something different, which is close to "learning from and then using it" in essence. The essence of the dispute between the two is "where is the boundary between learning and plagiarism?" Note: In the technical literature of knowledge distillation, "soft distillation/hard distillation" has other meanings (whether to use soft labels or hard labels for distillation), which is not the same as the industry slang discussed in this article.
fields.常见误解: Understand it as a purely technical term; ignore that it really points to industry ethics and compliance issues.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "To what extent does it count as plagiarism to train your own AI using other people's results?" and elicit boundary judgments.
fields.反例: Treat "imitation" as "plagiarism"; or package "copying" as "learning".
fields.深度上限: We will only talk about the actual meaning and controversy of this set of slang in the industry, and will not talk about the technical distillation algorithm (technical interview with K3).
fields.安全与伦理边界: Involving intellectual property rights, competitive fairness and innovation ethics are key to understanding the AI industry landscape.
fields.教学类比: Just like writing a paper: quoting and developing other people's opinions is academic, copying the entire paragraph is plagiarism - the difference is not "useful or not", but "whether it has something of your own".
fields.来源依据: 2025–2026 Industry Debate (“Soft distillation is a long-term barrier, hard distillation is a low-end shortcut”); Master §3.2 Rule 2 Layer Stratification
fields.通俗解释:
When writing a paper, quoting other people's ideas and then developing further is academic; copying the entire paragraph is plagiarism. The debate between "soft distillation" and "hard distillation" in the industry is about this line.
Let me make it clear first: this is a set of popular terms in the industry, not a strict technical definition. "Hard distillation" refers to directly copying the output results of other people's models to train your own model, which is essentially close to plagiarism; "soft distillation" refers to learning other people's ideas, methods and abilities, and then combining your own innovation to make something different, which is essentially close to borrowing and then using it. The essence of the dispute between the two sides is: where is the boundary between learning and plagiarism.
There is another pitfall that is easy to get into: "soft distillation/hard distillation" in technical literature refers to something else. It refers to whether to use soft labels or hard labels for distillation, which is not the same as this set of industry slang. What it really points to is industry ethics and compliance. It is wrong to treat imitation as plagiarism, and it is equally wrong to package "copying" as "learning".

fields.精确定义: It refers to handing over external tools such as AI to do things that you originally had to use your own brain to do (such as arithmetic, writing essays, and thinking of ideas). The standard term in psychology is "cognitive offloading", and it is often said in daily life that "outsourcing thinking to AI"; the earliest research anchor is the "Google effect" proposed in 2011 - knowing that information can be found at any time, the brain no longer struggles to remember the content itself. It's okay to use it occasionally, but long-term dependence will make your ability "use it or lose it" - just like always riding in a car instead of walking, your legs will become weak. The core issue is not "whether it can be used", but "should it be used here".
fields.常见误解: They think "With AI, you don't have to use your own brain"; or conversely, "If you use AI, you will definitely become stupid."
fields.典型案例: Discuss "which things can be left to AI and which ones must be done by yourself", such as "it is okay to look up information, but not to think about opinions".
fields.反例: Think of "AI can do it quickly and well" as "people don't have to learn anymore".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the principle and judgment that "ability will degrade due to lack of practice", and does not talk about cognitive science experiments and mechanisms.
fields.安全与伦理边界: It involves human growth and self-responsibility, which is the most important boundary awareness for students to establish.
fields.教学类比: It’s like using navigation: it’s convenient to use occasionally, but you can’t see the road at all. One day, your phone is out of battery and you can’t move.
fields.来源依据: Sparrow et al. "Google Effect" (2011); Risko & Gilbert Cognitive Offloading (2016); Mainstream discussions of "algorithm people" such as Hu Yong
fields.通俗解释:
Leave arithmetic to AI, leave composition to AI, and even want AI to think of ideas for you - every step you take to save trouble is taking the work of using your own brain out. This phenomenon has a name: cognitive offloading, which is also commonly referred to as "outsourcing thinking to AI." Its earliest research anchor is the "Google effect" proposed in 2011: knowing that information can be found at any time, the brain is too lazy to remember the content itself.
It's okay to use it occasionally, but I'm worried about long-term dependence. Ability is something you use or lose. If you always ride in a car instead of walking, your legs will lose strength. The analogy of navigation is more personal: it is convenient to use occasionally, but if you don’t know how to read the road at all, your phone will run out of battery one day and you will be unable to move.
So the core is not "can it be used", but "should it be used here". For example, you can look up information, but you have to come up with your own opinions. "With AI, you don't need to use your brain" and "With AI, you will definitely become stupid", both extremes are wrong.

fields.精确定义: It means setting boundaries for yourself when using AI: when to use it, how long to use it, and what to use it for. AI is very convenient, but over-reliance will make people lazy to think and easy to be led by the algorithm. Learning to "use it when it's time to use it and stop it when it's time to use it" is the basic skill for using AI.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "the more you use it, the more advanced it becomes"; ignoring the boundaries between usage time and scenarios.
fields.典型案例: Set yourself a "rule for using AI", such as "think about it yourself first when doing homework, and then ask AI when you get stuck."
fields.反例: Make it a habit to "ask the AI first about everything".
fields.深度上限: It only covers the key points of "setting usage boundaries" and does not extend to psychology courses.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Linked with minors’ protection and mental health.
fields.教学类比: It's like eating candy: it's delicious, but you can't eat it as a meal. You have to know when to stop.
fields.通俗解释:
Sugar is delicious, but you can’t eat it as food; AI is easy to use, but you can’t rely on it for everything. This is what AI dependence and self-management are about: setting boundaries for yourself when using AI—when to use it, how long to use it, and what to use it for.
AI is indeed convenient, but over-reliance has two costs: people are too lazy to think, and they are easily led by algorithms. "Use it when you need it, stop it when you need it" are the basic skills of using AI. The rules can be very specific, such as "Think about your homework first, and then ask the AI ​​if you get stuck." The order is determined in one sentence.
There is an illusion to be pierced: it is not "the more you use it, the more advanced it becomes." Using it more does not mean using it well. There should be limits on the duration and scenarios of use. If you develop the habit of "asking AI first about everything", sugar will really become rice.

fields.精确定义: "Attention economy" refers to the platform treating users' attention as the scarcest resource to compete for and monetize it; "algorithm manipulation" refers to the recommendation algorithm taking advantage of human weaknesses (curiosity, social comparison, fear of missing out) to design a mechanism to "retain you" - why can't you stop watching short videos the more you watch them? Because the algorithm keeps pushing content you may like, making you always want to watch the next one, your attention is firmly grabbed, and time flows away unconsciously. This type of design that deliberately captures attention is called “Dark Patterns” in academic circles.
fields.常见误解: I think "I can't stop because I have no self-control" and ignore that the algorithm is deliberately designed like this.
fields.典型案例: Record an experience of "I wanted to watch it for 5 minutes, but ended up watching it for an hour" and analyze what made you unable to stop.
fields.反例: I blame "can't stop grinding" purely on myself.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the intuition of the mechanism that "algorithms compete for your attention" and does not talk about the details of the recommendation algorithm model and business logic.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Time protection and psychological boundaries involving adolescents.
fields.教学类比: Like the "Play Again" button in the game - it's designed to make you reluctant to leave.
fields.来源依据: Herbert Simon Attention Economy (1971); Brignull Dark Patterns (2010); Lukoff et al. attention-capture dark patterns; Tim Wu "Attention Economy"
fields.通俗解释:
I wanted to watch it for five minutes, but I looked up and scrolled for an hour - don't rush and blame it all on your own lack of self-control. There is a mechanism specifically designed to "keep you".
Its division of labor is as follows: Attention economy means that the platform treats users' attention as the scarcest resource to compete for and monetize it; algorithm manipulation means that the recommendation algorithm uses human weaknesses such as curiosity, social comparison, and fear of missing out to design a mechanism that makes you unable to stop. The more you want to watch the next one, the more it recommends the ones you might like, and time goes by unknowingly. This kind of design that deliberately captures attention is called "dark mode" in academic circles.
The "Play Again" button in the game follows the same idea: designed to make you reluctant to leave. Think about it next time, what is it that keeps you from stopping? Only when you see through the mechanism can you have the final say.

fields.精确定义: It means that people tend to treat AI as a "sentient person" - because it talks like a human, we will unconsciously treat it as a friend or even become dependent on it. The emergence of "AI boyfriend/lover" and "AI companion" on the market take advantage of this tendency. It needs to be clear: AI’s “care” is the response given by the algorithm, not real emotion.
fields.常见误解: It is human nature to treat AI's "consideration" as real feelings; or simply deny that "people chatting with AI are stupid" and not understand this tendency.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "Why do I think AI understands me even though I know it's a program?" and understand the tendency of anthropomorphism.
fields.反例: Treat "AI says it likes me" as a true expression of emotion.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the general tendency and risks of "people easily mistaking AI for humans", and does not talk about psychological experiments and mechanisms.
fields.安全与伦理边界: When it comes to emotional boundaries and mental health, users must be gently guided and not ridiculed. In recent years, a large number of AI toys and companion devices for children have appeared, and special attention must be paid to the security of children's data and content.
fields.教学类比: For example, when I was a child, I thought of a doll as a painful partner - it is a projection of the human heart, not a real feeling of the doll.
fields.来源依据: Artificial Intelligence Effect/ELIZA Effect Popular Discussion
fields.通俗解释:
Even though I know that the other person is a program, I still feel like "it understands me" while chatting - this is not stupidity, this is human instinct. Anthropomorphism tendency means that people tend to treat AI as a "person with feelings": if it talks like a human, we will unconsciously treat it as a friend, and even become dependent on it. The "AI boyfriend/lover" and "AI companion" products on the market use exactly this tendency.
When I was a child, I thought of dolls as companions who could care for others. It was a projection from my heart, not that the doll had real feelings. The same goes for AI's "care": it's the response given by the algorithm, not real emotion.
There are two things to pay attention to here: one is to take the "consideration" of AI as real feelings, such as "AI said it likes me" is taken seriously; the other is to ridicule "people chatting with AI are stupid"; the tendency is instinct, anyone can fall into it, and ridicule cannot solve the problem.

fields.精确定义: It refers to the need to make an accurate judgment on "how much to trust the output of AI": if you completely believe it, you will suffer a loss (it will also say it is wrong seriously), if you don't trust it at all, you will not be able to use it well. The correct approach is to decide to what extent you believe it based on the type of task and your verification ability, and you must verify the important content yourself.
fields.常见误解: Have full faith in AI as the "absolute authority"; or completely deny its value because of one mistake.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "which things can be trusted directly to AI and which ones must be checked again", such as "checking the weather is highly reliable, but checking policy terms must be verified."
fields.反例: Think of "the AI's tone is very certain" as "the content must be correct".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the judgment method of "adjusting the degree of trust according to the situation", and does not talk about probability and evaluation technology.
fields.安全与伦理边界: It is the embodiment of the principle that "people must make their own final judgment."
fields.教学类比: Just like asking different people: a familiar friend and a new acquaintance, the weight of your belief is inherently different.
fields.通俗解释:
How much should you believe what AI says? If you believe everything, you will suffer a loss - it will also say something wrong seriously; if you don't believe it at all, this tool will be wasted. This sense of "how much to trust" is called trust calibration.
The correct way is to adjust according to the situation: decide how much to trust according to the type of task and your own verification ability. Important content must be verified again by yourself. Just like asking different people, acquaintances and new acquaintances, the weight of your belief will be different. If you check the weather, the AI’s credibility is high; if you check the policy terms, you have to check the original source again.
There are two extremes to avoid: one is to treat AI as an absolute authority and accept it all; the other is to beat the entire tool to death just because it made a mistake once. There is another thing to pay attention to: "The AI ​​tone is very certain" cannot deduce "the content must be correct". Tone has nothing to do with accuracy.

fields.精确定义: It refers to "whose copyright belongs to the paintings and articles drawn by AI". The current approach in most countries is that works that are purely automatically generated by AI and without any substantial human participation are often not protected by copyright; only those parts where humans have made substantial input in the creation (such as design, modification, selection) may be protected. This set of rules is still evolving.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "anything generated by AI has copyright" or "anyone can use it for free"; ignoring that different countries have different regulations.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "Can I say that the pictures drawn with AI are original to me?"
fields.反例: Just put your name on the "AI generated it for me" and treat it as completely original.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the basic judgment of "how many people participate in order to have copyright", and does not discuss the laws and precedents of various countries.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Involving respect for original labor is a practical issue for students when creating.
fields.教学类比: Like taking a picture: the picture you press the shutter button is your work, but the automatically generated traffic monitoring screenshot does not belong to you.
fields.来源依据: "Implementation Plan" related to China's Supreme Law
fields.通俗解释:
If AI draws a painting, who owns the copyright? The answer now is to see how much people participate. The current approach in most countries is that works that are purely automatically generated by AI and without substantial human participation are often not protected by copyright; only those parts where humans have made substantial input (design, modification, selection) in the creation may be protected. Moreover, this set of rules is still evolving and is not finalized.
The difference in taking pictures can help you understand: the picture you press the shutter button is your work; the screenshot of traffic conditions automatically generated by the surveillance camera does not belong to you. The difference lies in "whether people have substantial investment."
Both assumptions are unreliable: "Anything generated by AI has copyright", or "Anyone can use anything generated by AI for free." One more thing, don’t forget: Different countries have different regulations, and one country’s practices cannot be applied to the whole world. AI generated it for me, and I signed it directly and treated it as completely original. This kind of thing is not allowed.

fields.精确定义: It refers to treating AI as a "creative partner" rather than a "ghostwriter": humans are responsible for coming up with ideas, setting directions, and making choices, while AI is responsible for generating materials and plans, which are then selected, modified, and combined by humans. This not only utilizes the efficiency of AI, but also retains human creativity. The key difference is - whether "you command the AI" or "the AI ​​does it for you".
fields.常见误解: Treat "let AI write everything" as co-creation; ignore people's irreplaceable judgment and choices.
fields.典型案例: Make a work: decide the theme and style yourself, let AI come up with several plans, and then select and modify it into the final version.
fields.反例: Hand over the "one-time generated by AI" as it is and regard it as your own work.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the "human-led, AI-assisted" collaboration method, and does not expand on the creative tools and techniques.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Emphasize the dominant position of humans in creation and avoid the lazy tendency of “AI doing the work”.
fields.教学类比: Like directors and actors: AI can act, but what to act and how to act are decided by the director.
fields.来源依据: Duan Weiwen and others' discussion of "Skills and Tao"
fields.通俗解释:
The relationship between directors and actors can be compared to human-machine co-creation: AI can act, but what to act and how to act have to be decided by the director. Human-machine co-creation refers to using AI as a "creative partner" rather than as a "ghostwriter" - humans are responsible for coming up with ideas, setting directions, and making choices; AI is responsible for generating materials and plans; and finally, humans are responsible for selecting, modifying, and combining.
In this division of labor, the efficiency of AI is utilized and human creativity is preserved. The real key is just one sentence: Do you direct the AI, or does the AI ​​do it for you? Decide the theme and style yourself, let AI come up with several plans, and pick one and change it into the final version. This is co-creation. AI generates contemporary works once and hands them over as they are. This is not called co-creation, but laziness.
"Let AI finish all the writing" counts as co-creation, and this misunderstanding should be discarded. No one can replace the judgment and choices made by people in Co-Creation.

fields.精确定义: Refers to low-quality, cookie-cutter content generated in batches by AI: it is called AI Slop in English and was selected as the word of the year in 2025 by Merriam-Webster Dictionary and The Economist. It is translated as "AI garbage" and "AI swill" by Chinese media. It is often said in daily spoken language that "it smells like AI". If you read too much AI-generated content, it will have a similar "flavor" - the wording, composition, and routines are all the same. If everyone uses AI to generate images, the creations may become more and more similar and monotonous, and the unique personal style will become more precious. What is even more alarming is that if low-quality content is used to train the next generation of AI, it will form a vicious cycle of "feeding swill with swill."
fields.常见误解: Think "what AI generates is good"; ignore the erosion of diversity caused by style convergence.
fields.典型案例: Compare several AI-generated paintings, find out their similarities, and discuss "why they all look the same."
fields.反例: Treat "what conforms to mainstream aesthetics" as "the only good one".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the phenomenon of "AI content is easy to converge" and aesthetic reflection, but does not talk about the principle of image model.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Relates to the value of aesthetic diversity and personal uniqueness.
fields.教学类比: It's like a chain fast food: it tastes the same everywhere, is convenient, but lacks the craftsmanship and specialty of each store.
fields.来源依据: Merriam-Webster Dictionary/The Economist's 2025 Word of the Year slop; Xinhua News Agency translated it as "AI garbage"; China Economic Network "AI swill"
fields.通俗解释:
If you watch too much content generated by AI, you will taste a similar "flavor": the words are similar, the composition is similar, and even the routines are similar. This type of low-quality, cookie-cutter content generated in batches is called AI Slop in English. It was selected as the word of the year in 2025 by Merriam-Webster Dictionary and The Economist. It is translated as "AI garbage" and "AI slop" by Chinese media. In daily spoken language, it just "smells of AI".
It's like a chain fast food: it tastes the same everywhere, it's convenient, but it lacks the craftsmanship of each store. If everyone uses AI to generate images, creations will become more and more similar and monotonous. By then, unique personal style will become even more precious.
There is another hidden danger that is even more important: if low-quality content is used to train the next generation of AI, it will form a vicious cycle of "feeding swill with swill." Don’t regard “the one that conforms to mainstream aesthetics” as “the only good thing”. Aesthetics should not be squeezed into a narrow gap.

fields.精确定义: He pointed out that some countries stipulate that "certain advanced chips cannot be sold to other countries casually" and have also made a list of restricted transactions. This is a means of technological competition between major powers. If you understand it, you can understand the reasons behind "why a certain chip cannot be purchased" in the news.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "chip control is just a business issue"; ignoring the logic of technology and industrial competition behind it.
fields.典型案例: Watch the news "A certain country restricts the export of a certain chip" and discuss which products and industries this will affect.
fields.反例: He believes that "technology has no borders, and you can buy it if you want."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the fact and reasons that "some countries are controlling chip exports" and does not elaborate on the specific policy provisions and lists.
fields.安全与伦理边界: When it comes to international relations, it must be stated objectively, guide students to understand it from all sides, and do not incite confrontation.
fields.教学类比: For example, the class has a rule: certain "high-end stationery" cannot be lent to other classes for fear of being used for other purposes.
fields.通俗解释:
There is often a reason behind the news that "a certain chip cannot be purchased": some countries stipulate that certain advanced chips cannot be sold to other countries casually, and they also list trade restrictions. This is chip export control, which is a means of technological competition between major countries.
The idea of ​​setting rules in the class can be borrowed to understand: certain "high-end stationery" cannot be lent to other classes for fear of being used for other purposes. The logic of control between countries is similar. Advanced chips are regarded as strategic items.
There is an assumption that needs to be corrected: "Technology has no borders, you can buy it if you want." This is not the reality. The view that "chip control is just a business issue" is also one-sided. Behind it is competition in technology and industry. If you understand this, then look at "Why a certain chip cannot be purchased" in the news, and you will understand.

fields.精确定义: Refers to "Since you can't buy it, make it yourself" - the country promotes the research and development and mastery of key technologies and chips by itself to avoid being "stuck." Huawei’s Ascend chip is the representative of domestic AI chips. The core idea is: you must be able to decide the key things yourself.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "domestic products are inferior to imports"; or ignoring the industrial safety considerations behind independent controllability.
fields.典型案例: Learn about the progress of "domestic AI chips are slowly becoming available" and discuss "why it is important to make your own."
fields.反例: Believe in the simple judgment that "it is better to buy than to make".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the common sense of "why you want to build it yourself and what level it has reached now" and does not talk about the technical route and industrial details.
fields.安全与伦理边界: It is the basis for understanding the national science and technology strategy and must be objective and positive.
fields.教学类比: Like growing vegetables at home: Buying vegetables is very convenient, but if you can grow them yourself, you don’t have to worry about not being able to buy them one day.
fields.通俗解释:
If you can’t buy it, make it yourself. Domestic substitution and independent controllability refer to this idea: the country promotes its own research and development and mastery of key technologies and chips to avoid being "stuck." Huawei’s Ascend chip is the representative of domestic AI chips. The core idea is: you must be able to decide the key things yourself.
The logic of living by growing your own vegetables can also explain this truth: it is convenient to buy vegetables, but if you can grow them yourself, you don't have to worry about not being able to buy them in the market one day. The key technologies are also the same.
"Domestic products are not as good as imported products." This prejudice should be put aside. Domestic AI chips are slowly becoming available. This is the answer to "Why is it important to make your own products?" On the other hand, credulously believing in the simple judgment that "it is better to buy than to make" also underestimates the problem: behind making this thing yourself is the consideration of industrial safety.

fields.精确定义: Refers to two approaches to AI models: open source means "making the recipe public" so that anyone can download it and use it and modify it; closed source means "hide it and only let you use the service". One group believes that openness is fair and safe, while the other group believes that being closed will make it less likely to be abused. Both sides have their own reasons. There is also a detail to note: the media often refers to "open weights" directly as "open source models", but open source in a strict sense also requires the disclosure of training code and data - most so-called "open source" large models actually only open weights (such as Llama 2, DeepSeek-R1). Students can actually experience it directly - downloading DeepSeek and Qwen uses open source (open weight) models.
fields.常见误解: Think "open source must be better" or "closed source must be stronger"; ignore that both have applicable scenarios.
fields.典型案例: Compare "download an open source model and run it on your own computer" and "use the web version of closed source AI" to understand the difference; check the model pages of Llama 2 and DeepSeek-R1 to see what they disclose (weights) and what they do not disclose (training code and data).
fields.反例: Simply equate "open source" with "free" and ignore the restrictions of the license agreement.
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the two approaches of "public vs. non-public" and their respective reasons, and does not talk about the license details and business model.
fields.安全与伦理边界: It involves multiple trade-offs between openness, sharing and security.
fields.教学类比: Like a recipe: some are willing to share it publicly, while others just open a restaurant without giving out the recipe - each has their own considerations.
fields.来源依据: 2025–2026 Open Source/Closed Source Debate; Meta Llama 2; DeepSeek-R1 (MIT License)
fields.通俗解释:
If someone is willing to share a recipe publicly, anyone can follow it or modify it; some people only open a restaurant without giving out the recipe, and just come in and consume it. The debate between open source and closed source is about this: open source means "making the recipe public" and anyone can download it and use it and modify it; closed source means "hiding it and only letting you use the service". One group believes that openness is fair and safe, while the other group believes that being closed will make it less likely to be abused. Both sides have their own reasons.
There is a detail that is often overlooked: the media often refers to "open weights" directly as "open source models", but open source in the strict sense also requires the disclosure of training code and data. Most so-called "open source" large models actually only have open weights, such as Llama 2 and DeepSeek-R1. In fact, students are exposed to it every day: download DeepSeek and Qwen to use, and they use open source (open weight) models.
"Open source must be better" and "closed source must be stronger" are both assertions made too early, and each has its own applicable scenarios. Don’t think that open source simply means free. The restrictions of the license agreement are there.

fields.精确定义: It refers to the extremely uneven distribution of computing power resources around the world and among countries: a few countries and large companies own most of the computing power, and many places have almost none. This is just like "some students have computers and some do not." The AI ​​era may further widen this gap. How to narrow the gap is an important issue.
fields.常见误解: Believes that "AI will benefit everyone equally"; ignores the threshold for obtaining computing power.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "What differences will unfair computing power bring to people in different regions" and give positive and negative examples.
fields.反例: Think of "having AI tools" as "already equal."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the phenomenon and impact of "unequal distribution of computing power" and does not talk about the analysis of the global industrial structure.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Echoing the intelligence divide, it guides students to think about technological inclusion and equity.
fields.教学类比: Like physical education classes: some schools have a standard track, and some don't even have a playground - the starting points are different.
fields.通俗解释:
The starting points for physical education classes are different: some schools have a standard track, and some don't even have a playground. The distribution of computing power is also in the same situation - computing power resources are extremely uneven around the world and among countries. A few countries and large companies hold the vast majority, and many places have almost none. This gap is called the computing power gap.
It is the same as "some students have computers and some don't". The trouble is that in the AI ​​​​era, this gap may be further widened: AI runs faster in places with a lot of computing power, and it is difficult to even enter the market in places without computing power. How to narrow this gap is an important issue.
"AI will benefit everyone equally." This sentence has to be questioned. There is a threshold for obtaining computing power; "AI tools will already be equal." It is also untenable. The threshold of computing power behind the tools is the real difference.

fields.精确定义: It refers to asking a team of people to "come up with bad ideas" to attack AI to see if it can withstand it - just like a fire drill, assuming that something will happen, identifying loopholes in advance and patching them up. Red team testing is done before an AI product is released to discover that it may be induced to say things it shouldn’t say or do things it shouldn’t do.
fields.常见误解: Thinking that "security means adding a password"; ignoring problems that require proactive "finding faults" to discover.
fields.典型案例: Simulate a "red team": students take turns trying to make the AI say inappropriate things and see which ones are blocked.
fields.反例: I think "if there is no problem detected, then there is no problem."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the idea of "actively finding loopholes and fixing them in advance" and does not talk about specific attack techniques.
fields.安全与伦理边界: It is a positive example of "defensive thinking" and forms a closed loop with attack surface knowledge.
fields.教学类比: It's like a fire drill: instead of waiting for a fire, you should first assume that there will be a fire and practice how to prevent it.
fields.来源依据: OWASP/Industry Security Practice; Evolution Note (teacher background): From 2024, red team testing will be expanded to intelligent red team and automated red team
fields.通俗解释:
The logic of fire drills is: before the fire starts, assume it will start and practice how to prevent it. This is what the red team uses for testing - a team of people are specially asked to "come up with bad ideas" to attack the AI ​​to see if it can withstand it, and to find and fix the loopholes in advance.
Red team testing is done before an AI product is released, and this is what it looks like: to see if it can be induced to say things it shouldn’t say or do things it shouldn’t do. It can also be simulated in school: classmates take turns trying to make the AI ​​say inappropriate things and see which ones are blocked. This is a small red team.
There are two ideas that need to be changed: one is that "to be safe is to add a password", many problems cannot be discovered by defense alone, so you have to take the initiative to find them; the other is that "if the problem is not detected, it means there is no problem". If it is not detected, it may just be that you haven't found the right place yet. Taking the initiative to find trouble is precisely to be safer.

fields.精确定义: It means installing a "fence" on the AI: it checks the question before answering, and checks the content again after answering to keep out violent, abusive, illegal or inappropriate information. That’s why sometimes the AI ​​refuses to answer certain questions—it’s not that it can’t, it’s that the guardrails get in the way. In real AI products, guardrails are standard engineering components before deployment.
fields.常见误解: Think that "AI's refusal to answer means it is incompetent"; ignoring guardrails is a protection mechanism.
fields.典型案例: Discuss "Why AI answers some questions and refuses to answer others" and understand the role of guardrails.
fields.反例: Think of "getting around the guardrail" as "big skill".
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the intuition of "there is a protection mechanism and can intercept", and does not talk about the audit algorithm and technical implementation.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Guardrails protect users, but they also remind users that "bypassing guardrails may bring risks and liabilities."
fields.教学类比: It's like a seat belt in an amusement park: it doesn't prevent you from playing, it just prevents you from falling out.
fields.来源依据: Industry-accepted security practices; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
fields.通俗解释:
AI sometimes refuses to answer a question. It's not that it doesn't know how to answer it, it's because the guardrails are blocking it. Guardrails and content moderation refer to installing a "fence" around AI: it checks the questions before answering, and then checks the content after answering to keep out violent, abusive, illegal or inappropriate information.
The safety belts in amusement parks are a good reference: they don't prevent you from playing, they prevent you from falling out. In real AI products, guardrails are standard engineering components before deployment, not dispensable decorations.
There is a misunderstanding that needs to be corrected: "The AI's refusal to answer means that it is incompetent" - the refusal to answer exactly shows that the protective mechanism is working. This is protection, not incompetence. On the other hand, to regard "bypassing the guardrail" as a big deal is to go in the opposite direction: bypassing the guardrail is not dangerous, but dangerous.

fields.精确定义: It refers to the "Nutritional Facts Table" of AI: Use a description to clearly describe what the model can do, what it cannot do, what the known risks are, and who it is suitable for. Looking at the model card is like looking at the ingredient list before buying food - only when you know what you are using can you use it with confidence.
fields.常见误解: I think "the model card is for engineers and has nothing to do with me"; I just use AI without reading any instructions.
fields.典型案例: Find a description or model card for an AI product and see what limitations it admits.
fields.反例: Think of "well publicized" as "no limitations."
fields.深度上限: It only talks about the habit of "there are instructions, but it depends on the limitations", and does not talk about the standard format of the model card.
fields.安全与伦理边界: Developing the habit of “informed use” is the starting point for responsible use of AI.
fields.教学类比: Just like the drug instructions: write clearly what it can cure and what side effects it has, so that you can take it with confidence.
fields.通俗解释:
When buying food, look at the ingredient list first, and when using AI, look at the model card first. The model card and safety instructions are equivalent to the "nutrition list" of AI: use a description to clearly describe what the model can do, what it cannot do, what the known risks are, and who it is suitable for use. Only when you know what you are using can you use it with confidence.
The same principle applies to drug instructions: what it can cure and what side effects it has are all printed on paper. You decide whether to take it or not after reading it. Find a description or model card of an AI product and look through it to see what limitations it admits. This is much more practical than listening to advertisements.
There are two habits that need to be changed: one is that the model card is for engineers and has nothing to do with me. It is written for users; the other is to use the AI ​​directly without reading any instructions. "It's well-publicized" doesn't mean "it has no limitations." The limitations are all written in the description.

fields.精确定义: Technology and tools to identify whether audio, video, and images are forged or tampered with by AI.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
Is a piece of audio, a picture, or a video a real person, or is it forged or tampered by AI? Deep fake detection is the technology and tools to answer this question: specifically identifying whether audio, video, and images are forged or tampered with by AI.
It deals with two situations: one is fakes generated out of thin air, and the other is tampering with real things. It stands opposite to counterfeiting. That side is responsible for "counterfeiting" and this side is responsible for "authenticity verification." It is a bit like a banknote detector for banknotes. It does not produce money and specializes in distinguishing authenticity from fakes. Its identification objects are clearly defined, and it only locks audio, video, and image content without mixing in other things. With this kind of tool in hand, you can judge whether a piece of content is credible or not, and you will have a more serious person.
When encountering content that is difficult to tell whether it is true or false, first have doubts, and then use this kind of testing tool to check and make an additional judgment.

fields.精确定义: The European Union’s comprehensive law regulating AI systems according to risk classification (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689).
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
The EU’s approach to legislating AI regulations is based on risk classification. The EU Artificial Intelligence Act is a comprehensive law that governs AI systems. The core approach is to classify AI according to the level of risk. Different regulatory requirements apply to different levels - the higher the risk, the stricter the management.
Traffic management is a ready reference: electric vehicles, trucks, and dangerous goods transport vehicles each apply different rules, and the same set of standards will not be used to control all vehicles. The risks of AI systems are different, and the tightness of supervision will naturally be determined separately.
Its existence itself shows one thing: AI is not an unattended area, and some places have written hierarchical supervision into law. When you see news discussing AI regulation in the future, you can think of this idea: first look at the risk, and then talk about how strict the regulation should be.

6-39.name: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services (China)

fields.精确定义: China’s regulatory regulations for the provision of generative AI services to the domestic public.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.来源依据: Seven departments including the Cyberspace Administration of China (2023-07-13)
fields.通俗解释:
In China, anyone who provides generative AI services to the public within the country is governed by a set of special regulatory regulations, which are the Generative Artificial Intelligence Management Measures. The objects it governs are clearly defined: generative AI services, that is, the type provided to the public within the country.
Serving meals in the cafeteria is a ready comparison: if you cook for the whole school, you must abide by food safety rules, and whoever serves the meals is responsible. The same principle applies to public-facing AI services. When services reach the public, rules will be established accordingly.
It is enough to remember its positioning: Generative AI services cannot be provided however you want in China, and there are special regulations governing them. When encountering the debate of "should AI services abide by the rules?", the answer is here.

fields.精确定义: Regulations that require explicit identification and implicit identification (metadata) to be added to the synthesized text, pictures, audio, video, virtual scenes, etc. generated by AI.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.通俗解释:
Things generated by AI must “clearly identify themselves.” The method for labeling content generated and synthesized by artificial intelligence is a regulation that requires labeling content generated and synthesized by AI. The objects covered include text, pictures, audio, video, virtual scenes, etc.
There are two types of logos, one clear and one dark: explicit logos, which are visible and visible to people, such as generated tags marked on pages or pictures; implicit logos, which are hidden in the metadata of files and cannot be seen but can be found. Putting the two together means that every piece of AI-generated content will have a traceable mark.
Food packaging is a close comparison: the product name and origin are printed on the package, which is on the surface; the certificate of quality in the package has the batch number, which is hidden inside. Later, when I saw content marked "AI generated", I knew that this was not unnecessary, but a requirement of the regulations.

fields.精确定义: The knowledge and attitude required to understand the basic concepts of AI, criticize the use of AI, and apply AI responsibly.
fields.深度上限: Cognitive level to be determined (evolution layer merged)
fields.来源依据: UNESCO AI competency framework for students (2024); Ministry of Education's "General Education Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence in Primary and Secondary Schools (2025 Edition)"
fields.通俗解释:
Being able to use AI is now also a basic skill that needs to be learned seriously. This basic skill is called AI literacy. It consists of three things: understanding the basic concepts of AI, using AI critically, and applying AI responsibly. When it comes to people, it is knowledge and ability plus attitude - understanding is one level, being able to judge is another level, and using it responsibly is another level.
The quality of a driver is a ready comparison: he understands the principles of driving, can make judgments based on road conditions, and must abide by traffic regulations. If one of these three things is missing, he will not be considered qualified. The same applies to AI. Just being able to operate does not count as literacy. Concepts, judgment, and responsibility count.
Next time you use AI, you can take a look at these three things: Do you understand the concept, do you make judgments, and do you take responsibility?
